article_title: A celebration of diamonds for the bride redefining traditions
sub_title: Tanishq’s Rivaah and Tarun Tahiliani present a bridal collection where diamonds shine for the modern bride
article_content: There’s a reason diamonds have been treasured across centuries—their brilliance goes beyond the visual. Forged deep within the Earth over billions of years, each natural diamond is a marvel of time, pressure, and precision. They’ve adorned everything from ancient talismans to royal crowns, embodying power, mystique, and legacy. In modern times, their allure has evolved, resonating with a generation that values both individuality and tradition. Recently, Tanishq and De Beers joined hands to celebrate this timeless appeal with an extraordinary event: Pride of Tanishq. This immersive experience paid tribute to natural diamonds, their unparalleled beauty, and their enduring legacy. The event unfolded as an intimate journey through the story of diamonds. Guests were greeted by a captivating zone that took them from the very core of the Earth to the refined brilliance of a polished gem. Imagine a 360-degree Van Gogh-inspired experience where the formation of diamonds came to life, making visitors feel as though they’d stepped into the heart of the Earth itself—where diamonds are formed over billions of years. They’re brought to the surface by rare volcanic eruptions through kimberlite conduits. This geological serendipity transforms carbon into one of nature’s rarest treasures. But the magic doesn’t stop there. From mine to masterpiece, each rough diamond is meticulously sorted, then cut and polished to reveal its breathtaking brilliance. Master craftsmen breathe life into these raw stones, creating pieces that reflect beauty, strength, and timelessness. Like fingerprints, no two diamonds are the same, making each one as unique as the individual who wears it. The journey continued with a second zone dedicated to the cornerstone of diamond evaluation—the 4Cs. Buying natural diamonds can feel overwhelming with all the technical jargon, but decoding gemstone certificates is simpler than it seems once you know what to look for. These certifications detail the grading of a diamond based on specific attributes. By understanding these key qualities, you’ll not only appreciate the stone’s unique beauty but also its value as defined on paper. Through immersive displays, the second zone was dedicated to demystifying what makes a diamond truly exceptional. At Tanishq, all the diamonds are selected and sorted with utmost care and stringent processes giving a Tanishq diamond the best sparkle. Together, these characteristics offer a roadmap to finding a diamond that’s a perfect companion for you. The final zone showcased the extraordinary artistry of Tanishq. Collections like Ethereal Wonders showcased rare diamonds and varied designs, Celeste Solitaires boasted fine solitaires, and Enchanted Trails highlighted how natural diamonds are transformed into wearable art. Speaking of Tanishq's artistry, this season, Rivaah collaborates once again with celebrated designer Tarun Tahiliani to unveil the second edition of Rivaah x Tarun Tahiliani, a collection that celebrates the evolving narrative of the contemporary Indian bride. Building on the success of their inaugural collaboration, this latest line-up is inspired by the poetic intricacies of the This collection is crafted to resonate with the modern Indian bride who seamlessly weaves heritage with modernity. This collection of over 80 designs—spanning chokers, When it comes to choosing the perfect diamond, price isn’t the only thing to be considered—quality and authenticity are non-negotiable, and brands like Tanishq adhere to the highest standards. Diamonds are enduring symbols of history, each carrying a story of beginnings and moments frozen in time. It’s this narrative, etched into their very core, that makes them forever.

Designers of the era, such as Calvin Klein and Jil Sander, championed the clean lines and easy wear of the bias-cut slip. Whether rendered in liquid silk, matte satin or cut from daring sheer fabrics, the slip skirt has become a foundational wardrobe piece that anchors spring outfits. article_content: For a close friend’s wedding, Aditi Rao Hydari wore a handwoven Kanjeevaram silk sari by Gaurang Shah, built around a high-voltage pairing of lime green, royal purple and antique gold. The sari’s broad gold zari pallu and hem do most of the visual work, giving the drape heft and shine, while the body stays lighter with scattered butis across the lime silk. The purple edge tracing the sari sharpens the contrast further, and the blouse picks that thread up exactly. Cut in the same saturated purple with woven gold detailing, it holds the palette together. In profile, the silk falls with the dense, sculpted drop Kanjeevaram does so well, especially around the lower half, where the pleats open into that unmistakable temple-silk sweep. She kept the jewellery traditional and close to the fabric language, with jhumkas, stacked bangles and a gemstone-set choker that sits neatly at the neck. Charlotte Wang styled Hydari’s hair in a half-up look and kept the makeup fresh, with flushed cheeks and a nude lip. “This look is a masterclass in colour blocking without looking like a statement. The gold jewellery supplements the undertones of the neon and the borders of the kanjeevaram sari. Add a dash of white to heighten the freshness of the look; one white gold bangle on each hand would go a long way,” says Manglien Gangte, Vogue India fashion associate.

Swap the slip-on wedges for a pair of juttis,” says Manglien Gangte, Vogue India's fashion associate.

article_title: Priyanka Chopra Jonas returns to the Oscars 2026 in a white Dior gown with a feather-trimmed slit
sub_title: A sculpted bodice and diagonal draping through the waist shape the white gown’s streamlined silhouette
article_content: Priyanka Chopra Jonas returned to the Oscars red carpet in a white Dior gown that moves from a sharply cut bodice into a fluid skirt. The strapless neckline curves into an angular sweetheart shape, while the bodice holds firm through the waist. Below, the dress changes direction as fabric gathers diagonally across the hips, drawing the eye toward one side before falling into the skirt. That shift introduces movement through the midsection and breaks the straight line of the bodice. A high slit runs through the skirt, edged with feather trimming along the opening. The feathers sit only along that cut of the fabric rather than across the entire skirt, forming a narrow band of texture against the white base. As Chopra Jonas walked the carpet and later stepped on stage to present, the feathered edge lifted and settled with her stride. She wore high jewellery from Bvlgari’s Eclecttica collection, including a diamond necklace set with a vivid blue centre stone and matching rings. Her hair was worn long and sleek with a side part, brushed over one shoulder. The makeup followed a warm, muted palette: softly smoked eyes, bronzed skin and a nude lip. Nick Jonas accompanied her in a Ralph Lauren tuxedo jacket with a white shirt and black bow tie. Chopra Jonas last attended the Oscars nearly a decade ago. Her return this year favoured clean tailoring and controlled texture over elaborate embellishment, allowing the silhouette and the feathered movement of the skirt to register from a distance. “Rethink the white gown for a corporate outing, opt for a white suit and if you want to add a little bit of play, you can don a suit with a feather trim on the sleeve hem. The sleekness or sharpness of the look depends on the cut of the suit and the clean lines. Opt for trousers that are straight, slim-legged, and fall over your stilettos. A clean watch and an ear cuff to complete the look,” says Divya Balakrishnan, Vogue India fashion associate.

article_title: Sharvari’s Torani lehenga showcased 2,000 hours of zardozi, dapka and marodi handwork
sub_title: The actor’s lotus pink and sage lehenga was paired with jewellery by Sunita Shekhawat
article_content: At a wedding reception where moody and metallic tones typically dominate after dark, Sharvari made a case for the softer side of eveningwear. The actor's pastel lehenga by Torani is proof that powdery palettes can hold their own. The lehenga is crafted in raw silk and complemented with a scalloped blouse with full sleeves and a translucent sage organza dupatta. For designer Karan Torani, the inspiration lies deep within Indian mythological storytelling. “This ensemble draws its spirit from the eternal poetry of Raas Leela, the divine dance of Radha and Krishna that has lived for centuries in Indian miniature paintings, temple murals and oral folklore,” he says. “I was imagining Radha standing quietly by the banks of the Yamuna in Vrindavan, a figure suspended between devotion and romance, surrounded by blooming gardens, peacocks and the music of the flute.” That imagery informed the soft lotus pink and sage colours of the garment. Torani envisioned the outfit “to feel almost like an Indian figurine coming to life,” he explains. The silhouette, too, borrows from historical Indian dress forms. “The choli draws from the classic angiya, a form that has existed in Indian dress traditions for centuries, interpreted with gentle, sculpted cuts to give it a contemporary elegance while retaining its modest, full-sleeved romanticism.” Across the lehenga, Torani’s signature visual language appears through scalloped borders, chintz florals and the Airavata elephant motif. Equally compelling is the surface ornamentation on the lehenga. “The entire surface is enriched with traditional hand techniques–zardozi, dapka, marodi, badla and kinari work–each painstakingly layered by artisans who have inherited these skills across generations. When these techniques come together, the garment begins to feel less like fabric and more like a tapestry,” Torani reveals. The process required more than 2,000 hours of handwork, with every scallop and motif positioned deliberately. “A small detail that brings it all together is the heart-shaped ‘Dilbar’ potli.” Styled by Tanya Ghavri, Sharvari’s lehenga was completed with jewellery from Sunita Shekhawat. Pieces from the Jaipur-based label’s Padmapriya collection brought in lotus and parrot motifs inspired by Goddess Lakshmi. Her chandbalis with kaan phool showcased intricate champlevé and delicate gulabi meenakari and they were paired with a ring from the label’s Heritage collection.

article_title: From Cloud Dancer to power blue, 10 colour trends dominating the runways right now
sub_title: Vogue brings you the colour trends of note for 2026
article_content: As something of a maestro when it comes to setting colour trends, Interestingly, this creamy note somewhat preempted But, of course, what might be a succour to one person, enabling them to feel cool, calm and collected, could simply be, well, slightly boring to someone else, who perhaps feels invisible or even sad in stealth-wealth neutrals. Luckily, the spring/summer 2026 collections didn’t just cater to one school of thought but, instead, offered up multiple colour theories for contemplation. Prada’s show contained typically “off” gradations, including, but not limited to, canary yellow, lime green and turquoise blue. Naturally, they did the job of making certain garments – fluid knee-length skirts attached to a set of braces or, equally, knickers with a pair of pockets on either side – look even more outlandish (and brilliant, obviously). Elsewhere, bold colour-blocking was interspersed with easy-to-wear shades like black, white and chocolate. This was very much present and correct at It would also be remiss not to consider the most recent autumn/winter 2026 runways, which confirmed that bold colour will be everywhere at the tail end of the year too. It’s one thing to appreciate a colour as it comes down the catwalk. But, as easy as it might be to get swept up in a designer’s singular vision, recasting your wardrobe in electrically-charged hues as opposed to basic navy or beige, it will first pay to consider what colours feel like “you”. To help, we’ve dissected 10 colour trends that you could add to your roster ahead of the new season. Fuchsia made its presence felt on the catwalk at Alaïa, where a knitted skirt, falling in asymmetric pleats that zig-zagged up one calf, was the definition of “hot pink.” And it didn't stop there. At Chloé, puff-sleeved fuchsia crop tops were somewhat neutralised by sensible khaki skirts. Meanwhile over at Conner Ives, the shade was practically top-to-toe, with one outfit comprising a collar-popped tracksuit top, a fringed skirt and toe-thong Prada is always one-to-watch for what trends will cut through over the next six months, not least because of the way Ms. Prada manages to make any colour an interesting proposition (even the brand’s actual runway was a glossed clementine orange). Despite the profusion of shades, it was this particular Jil Sander’s spring/summer 26 collection was a lesson in “less is more”, with a focus on Klein Blue, a saturated primary-coloured shade that appeared on single-breasted coats, soft-power dresses and cropped jumpers. Eye-popping in some ways, but grounded in others, you won’t regret inviting its exuberance into your wardrobe, as long as it’s tempered by opaque black tights or a wool skirt in white. Tomato is a non-mover when it comes to colour trends – but for spring/summer 26, there’s a twist. At We’ve already discussed the relevance of Pantone’s “ For one of the most exciting debuts at Paris Fashion Week, Loewe’s creative-director duo, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, delivered something of a wham-bam colour palette featuring searing primary shades. This green – or more accurately emerald – was particularly head-turning, especially when rendered as this clean take on While navy has long been a mainstay of the modern wardrobe, the autumn/winter 2026 collections offered elevated new interpretations of the shade. At Burberry, it appeared across an entire spectrum of textures, from plissé taffeta to buttery leather accessories, proving how much depth a single hue can hold. Ferragamo and If fuchsia is the grown-up way to wear pink, bubble gum is its playful younger sibling. Designers embraced the saccharine shade in glossy fabrics and sharply-cut silhouettes, giving the Barbie-approved hue a fresh dose of fashion credibility. At A softer alternative to navy, powder blue emerged as a key transitional shade across both seasons. At Chanel, it softened the house’s signature tweeds and polished accessories, while Erdem applied it to fluid silks adorned with delicate embroidery and embellishment. There’s an inherent calmness to powder blue, but in 2026, it feels far from sleepy. Styled alongside deeper blues, rich reds, chocolate browns or flashes of pink, the shade becomes quietly powerful. At Marni, Meryll Rogge’s highly anticipated debut as creative director set the tone with a palette of pastels punctuated by bursts of brightness. Among the standouts was butter yellow, a shade that has been steadily gaining traction for several seasons. Look out for creamy-toned variations rather than acidic brights. When styled with chocolate brown, navy or cream, butter yellow behaves almost like a neutral, which is precisely what makes it one of the most wearable colour trends of the year.

article_title: Why a generation raised on screens is getting into watches
sub_title: Rado’s Adrian Bosshard shares what brands are learning from a new generation of collectors
article_content: I got my first real watch when I was about 10—a Casio F-91W that was a gift from my father. It was my introduction to ‘real’ watches as opposed to the cheap knockoffs I had worn before. It was only in my 20s that I bought a watch with my own money, a Tissot PR100 that required a serious squeeze from my wallet. But it was worth every penny. It turns out that story isn’t unique, with Gen Z collectors beginning their careers today and finding themselves in the same boat. Having been introduced to the watch world at a young age by the adults in their lives—or discovering it through its adjacency with their other interests—they are now beginning to build collections of their own. “The beginning of my obsession started when my grandfather passed on a Citizen Signature chronograph to me,” says 23-year-old Nirek Dembla, a student of business analytics. He adds, “I was instantly fascinated with its engineering and proportions; the dial taught me about the elegance of smaller dial sizes.” Archana Ajith, a 28-year-old journalist from Mumbai, credits her father for shaping her interest. “He has an extensive watch collection and began building it when he was around my age. Growing up, I watched him carefully choose each piece with a deep appreciation for its craftsmanship.” Twenty-eight-year-old Gladwin Menezes, however, developed his obsession independently. “[It’s] something I cultivated by watching tennis matches and sporting events where athletes would wear cool watches. Eventually, I grew curious about why their watches cost so much; despite the jokes about ‘time toh same hi dikhata hai’, I wanted to understand the craft, history and also a little about the mechanics.” That joke about watches has been around for decades. My X-rupee watch tells the same time as your a-lot-more-than-X-rupee one. And the response hasn’t changed either: a watch does more than tell time. It can speak volumes about whether you value attention to detail or vibes; prefer unabashed bling or stoic restraint; are interested in craft or technology, maybe both. A report from Chrono24 and Fratello from last year revealed that Gen Z watch owners around the world are drawn to vintage dress watches. Many of these have become familiar sights on social media feeds and red carpets alike, being sported by pop-culture figures from Zohran Mamdani with his Casio A1000MA-7VT to Saif Ali Khan’s Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso Grande Taille and Paul Mescal’s Cartier Tank. For many young collectors, these pieces become entry points into watch history. “What particularly draws me to the Cartier Tank is its proportions, as it proves that a watch does not need to be massive to have a presence,” says Dembla. Menezes concurs: “The Tank has always been a favourite, and the Reverso is also one that I find really interesting.” India’s most famous defunct watchmaker also continues to attract Ajith. “I admire vintage HMT mechanical timepieces because they represent a period when India had its own watchmaking identity.” Luxury watch imports into India have been steadily rising in recent years, with a combined increase of 35% according to reports from Deloitte and Morgan Stanley-LuxeConsult. A new free-trade agreement between India and the EU will gradually reduce import duties on Swiss watches, potentially expanding the market further. Among the brands paying attention to this growing interest is Rado. I recently met CEO Adrian Bosshard, who was in the country for the launch of the True Round x Les Couleurs Le Corbusier collection at India Art Fair; the watchmaker has had a presence at the Delhi event for seven years. Bosshard (the perfect example of nominative determinism, if ever there was one) was eager to discuss what the company has observed among younger buyers, a target market that continues to grow. He reveals, “We’re seeing an important trend with young customers—of [them buying] long-term luxury goods. Today, young customers think and evaluate [their options]; they like to buy products with a long-term and sustainable relevancy.” When asked about timeless vintage designs, Bosshard points to the Anatom, a 40-year-old icon that was revived a few years ago. “It was a total revolution at the time [in 1983] because of its design. At a time when watches were round and steel, it was ‘Hardmetal’ (Rado’s proprietary tungsten-carbide alloy) and anatomical.” The curvature of the watch was designed to enhance its wrist-feel—one of the factors Bosshard considers when choosing a watch, alongside design, quality and reliability. Our Gen Z contributors seem to echo this list. “Proportions are very important; a watch has to sit well on my wrist and feel balanced,” Ajith says. Dembla concurs: “I mainly focus on sub-40mm watches as I think they provide the most balanced silhouette [for me],” adding, “I also look for clean, minimal designs that are backed by rich historical significance.” These criteria are mirrored in their collections and wishlists. Dembla says, “My most recent and significant piece is a Rado Captain Cook high-tech ceramic diver with a beautiful green dial. This watch in particular was the grail for me when I started collecting, because of its concave ceramic bezel and pure diver-watch DNA. As for what’s next in my collection, it’s a Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso.” Ajith’s wish list also features names that will be instantly recognisable to collectors of any age: “Audemars Piguet and Cartier will probably always be on it. But realistically, what I’m eyeing right now is a 37mm Rado Captain Cook automatic.” For this new wave of collectors, the watches on their wish lists share one thing in common: longevity. While trends may ebb and flow, these are pieces chosen with the expectation that they will stay meaningful long after the novelty of purchase fades. As Dembla puts it, “In a time when we are surrounded by vast amounts of fleeting digital utility, a traditional timepiece acts as a rare island of permanence.”

article_content: Suhana Khan made her way to the wedding ceremony of Arjun Tendulkar and Saaniya Chandhok in Mumbai on Thursday alongside her parents, Shah Rukh Khan and Gauri Khan. For the occasion, the actor chose a romantic pastel lehenga by The look leaned entirely into spring-summer’s most covetable language: a pastel palette and an abundance of florals. At weddings where maximalism is often the dress code, her look took the season-appropriate approach of choosing something fun and fresh over heavy opulence. The lehenga set comprised a cap-sleeved blouse with a sweetheart neckline paired with a voluminous, floor-sweeping skirt and a wispy dupatta. The skirt featured alternating panels of kalis in shades of blush pink and mint green, which create a subtle contrast and visual intrigue. Embroidery played a pivotal part in bringing the ensemble to life. The entire lehenga was doused in thread embroidery that rendered delicate florals and foliage motifs across the surface in a painterly arrangement. The placement of the motifs allowed the skirt to feel richly detailed without appearing dense. Injecting contrast and an ethereal movement to the blush lehenga was a butter yellow organza dupatta. The pop of colour broke the pink monotony and was draped loosely over one shoulder. Along with the same thread embroidery on the lehenga, the dupatta was punctuated with rich zardozi work. Ami Patel styled the look with a multi-hued gemstone necklace and matching drop earrings. Her makeup was minimal, featuring a dewy base and rose pink hues on the eyes and lips. Her blow-dried hair was styled into soft curls in a half-up-half-down style and finished with a small bouquet of fresh flowers.

article_title: Ananya Panday’s gold-thread Anamika Khanna couture and Priyanka Chopra Jonas’s layered Dior skirt lead this week’s best looks
sub_title: Texture and tailoring take the lead, with embroidery-heavy couture sitting alongside runway-driven silhouettes
article_content: Surface work, tailoring and silhouette shifts defined this week’s standout fashion moments. Embroidery dominated the Indian looks, from Ananya Panday’s densely worked Anamika Khanna couture to Mrunal Thakur’s paisley-laden sari by Mrunalini Rao. Elsewhere, international runways entered the mix: Alia Bhatt stepped out at Milan Fashion Week in a leather trench worn as a dress, while Priyanka Chopra Jonas attended Dior’s show in Jonathan Anderson’s layered skirt silhouette referencing Paul Poiret. Ananya Panday wore Anamika Khanna couture in the form of a mandarin-collar jacket and long skirt densely covered in gold floral embroidery. Vines, leaves and blossoms spread across the surface in layered threadwork with sequins and bead clusters stitched through the motifs, giving the garment a richly worked texture. Along the inner closure running down the front of the jacket, strings of white beads formed scalloped edges that introduced a lighter vertical line through the field of gold. From the jacket hem, long strands of fringe fell over the skirt and moved with each step, bringing motion to a surface otherwise packed with ornamentation. Stylist Priyanka Kapadia Badani paired the ensemble with a neckpiece built around fan-shaped motifs and stud earrings, but it is the pearl drops on the necklace that create continuity with the ensemble's surface work. Riviera Lynn created a luminous no-makeup makeup look, while hair by Sankalp Vilas Surve fell in loose waves that softened the sharp neckline of the mandarin collar. Sanya Malhotra chose an Aseem Kapoor ensemble built around a sculpted bra blouse embroidered with figurative motifs and geometric borders. The skirt extended the palette through vertical panels worked with resham thread, zari and marori embroidery, with bead tassels and small hanging details scattered across the surface. A printed dupatta in sheer silk introduced another layer of pattern to the mix of colour and texture. article_title: 5 Vogue-approved low-effort style hacks for the tired girl
sub_title: Take it from one very tired stylist
article_content: When you’re tired, decision fatigue is real. On mornings when you’re running on Over time, I’ve realised that looking put together has very little to do with effort. The best low-effort style hacks aren’t about buying more; they’re about building a system you can rely on when your brain refuses to cooperate. Build a uniform wardrobe with a neutral palette (or any other colour scheme that works for you), one ‘personality piece’ and a signature scent to seal it. For me, that’s a pair of wide-fit Uniqlo trousers from the women’s section that I have in three colours, ribbed tanks in black and white and a rotation of button-downs, shackets, kimonos and tang jackets, topped off with a baseball cap and a few spritzes of Another 13 by Le Labo. I could pick anything from this pile blindfolded and they’d appear just as thought out because these are all foundational pieces that have helped me create an OOTD stencil for mornings that just aren’t it. Here's a list of 5 very low-effort styling hacks that will make you look undeniably tasteful. Hair accessories are the easiest form of maximalism and are your best friends for days you don't have the time or energy to wash or dress it up. One large, colourful scrunchie instantly shifts the energy of an outfit. If you don't have the hair length for a scrunchie, throw a baseball cap on. You can wear the simplest outfit in the world, jeans and a white shirt or a simple A-line dress that doesn't need ironing and still look like a style savant if you do your hair right. Metallic accents are the tired girl’s shortcut to looking awake. Think of metal as Even if you've spent hours putting your look together, the wrong choice of footwear can flush it all down the drain. A pair of well-made shoes, whether they're sneakers or a pair of embroidered Nothing screams tired and busy (and stylish) girlie than a bag that holds your entire universe in it. Call it the Jane Birkin-fication of your low-effort look. Step out in your pyjamas if you have, carry the right arm candy and you're set. Just say, “Claire, it's French!” Sometimes, the best beauty hack for a tired face is to cover up the eyes. And if you're anything like me, your patience disintegrates the more tired you are. And to be honest, it is smarter to hide those tired glares before it becomes occupational hazard.

article_title: Mrunal Thakur’s salmon Chanderi anarkali layers digital jaal with hand-finished aari edges
sub_title: Stepping out for her latest rom-com promotions, the actor embraced spring-ready florals with her salmon pink Ri By Ritu Kumar set
article_content: Mrunal Thakur has been out and about for the promotions of a newly-released rom-com, The salmon pink anarkali features a delicate floral jaal rendered through digital printing. Cut with Chanderi silk fabric, the full-sleeved kurta is designed with a fitted yoke that opens into a generous flare that’s composed of alternating kalis in varied floral prints. Each kali is edged with intricate aari work, adding texture and definition to the billowing silhouette. The V-neckline yoke, sleeves and bodice are accented with hand-embroidery, sequins and aari work tracing the striking bloom motifs. The set is paired with a classic churidar that streamlines the volume of the kurta,  and overlayed is an organza dupatta scattered with fine golden dots and edged with lace. What makes the actor’s ensemble compelling is its versatility. Starting with the wispy textile, which is often touted as “bunni hui hawa” or handwoven air by master weavers. Chanderi silk’s subtle inherent shimmer and breathable construction make it the perfect pick for the often muggy Indian weather. You can sport it at daytime outings just as you can for intimate wedding events. The salmon pink shade, too, flatters across seasons and occasions. The best part about an anarkali set, like Thakur’s, is that you can easily tilt the outfit’s mood with some smart styling. The right jewellery and makeup can dial it up or down. Where Thakur chose drop earrings set with rubies to accessorise the ensemble for a daytime outing, a choker would instantly make it festive-appropriate. For footwear, she went with Kolhapuri block heels and kept the beauty look soft with an old rose lipstick, mascara-laden lashes and a gentle flush on the cheeks.

article_content: Bhumi Pednekkar’s House of Kotwara chogha doesn’t behave like the versions it references. The length and layering remain, but the organza is sheer and the front is left open. A bandeau angia cuts a clean line across the torso, exposing a strip of skin where you would expect coverage. The Chikankari is carried through every layer in white-on-white thread, so the surface feels continuous even as the garments separate. The silhouette moves between overlay and base instead of settling into one shape. Styled by Manisha Melwani, the jewellery restores ceremony at the neckline. Ruby earrings and an oxidised hathphool from Harubhai Zaveri extend the detail outward, while saharas from Shrihari Diagems add another line of ornament. Hair by Jyoti Mandre is pulled back, keeping the jewellery uninterrupted. The smoky eye and small black bindi hold their own against the tonal white. “What stands out is the sheer beauty and the handwork, the way the look has been subtly layered also adds to the richness of this silhouette. To make this your own work with an Indian choli or bralette with embroidery work, and can layer it with an overlay or angrakha tied loosely to emphasise the blouse. Work on a white-on-white layering like Bhumi Pednekkar to achieve this Indian ethereal look,” says Vogue India fashion associate Divya Balakrishnan.

article_title: Bhumi Pednekkar aces Regencycore in a pastel Shehla Khan lehenga
sub_title: The actor’s lavender ensemble draws from period references and remains rooted in Indian occasion wear
article_content: For a friend’s destination wedding, Bhumi Pednekkar championed Regency era romance in a pastel lehenga. Part of Shehla Khan's latest couture collection, her ensemble felt like it had been pulled directly from the pages of a True to the collection's title, Romance Reimagined, Khan revisits the codes that first defined her eponymous label. “The idea behind each look of this collection was to go back to the original aesthetic of the brand. The textures, soft prints and intricate detailing come together to create unique and feminine styles that can be worn through years and seasons,” reveals Khan. A soft lavender print of large roses is emblazoned across a fluid lehenga skirt. “This lehenga skirt is paired with a bustier style blouse inspired by the romance of Victorian style with a lingerie-esque detail and embroidered buttons.” The blouse, with its scalloped lace neckline, structured printed cups, sensual open back and delicate buttons, brings corsetry codes into the Indian occasion conversation without feeling costume-driven. Puffed sleeves in sheer lace lend volume at the shoulder, further reinstating Regency silhouettes. “The dupatta, which is coordinated with the print of the lehenga and lace of the blouse, amplifies its lightness and adds the traditional touch,” adds Khan. Pednekkar’s stylist, Nidhi Jeswani, accessorised her look with a pair of chandbali earrings and a ring from Shri Paramani Jewels. Pednekkar braided her hair with lace trims, reinforcing the romantic mood. Regency era style romanticises femininity through flirty florals, fine trims and floaty silhouettes. In recent seasons, designers and celebrities have embraced these elements, translating historical cues into modern wardrobes. Pednekkar’s lehenga interpretation demonstrates how those references can be seamlessly adapted into Indian festive dressing.

article_title: Is the male gaze evolving?
sub_title: Sometimes I dress like a boy, but my straight boyfriend still thinks I look cute
article_content: My Fast-forward 18 months, and my style has only become more ‘tomboy femme’. My jeans are baggier than ever. I own more vests and structured tops than I need. And yet, my skirt collection is at an all-time high (I now own four). If you happen to rummage through my wardrobe, you'll see lace and frills peeking through. I dress based on how I’m feeling—whether that’s a basic tank top and Which raises the question: are men evolving? Is the male gaze loosening its grip on the deep cleavage and hip-hugging silhouette? Or have some men simply learned to see fashion as expression, an extension of the women they love? “I’m not really going to change myself to make someone I’m dating more comfortable,” shares New York–based creator Teo Marcella. Marcella, who is in a four-year relationship with their boyfriend, admits there was temptation in the beginning to lean into dressing a certain way, but they pushed against it. “I held my own ground in what I knew was comfortable for me. And I think, honestly, that authenticity has allowed us to develop a really strong foundation.” Marcella grew up with a very specific kind of femininity. “As a kid, I was very girly, looking at the stars of Disney Channel. It was all very feminine.” But with time, they realised they felt “so much more comfortable and so much more in my body dressing androgynously. I still like to have a feminine face, but I love a masc outfit,” shares Marcella. Interestingly, they notice how the world responds. “When I’m dressed more masculine, there’s less chivalry from people around. People might hold doors for me less [often], but I’ll hold doors [open] for people. I’ll help people out of cars. Something interesting happens with my energy there.” Aastha Gaur, a Los Angeles–based creator and senior director of design at Google, describes her style as existing between chill and commanding, rather than feminine or masculine. “Imagine a T-shirt and jeans,” she says. “More chill would be wearing a cardigan. More commanding would be wearing a Growing up in India, Gaur identified as a tomboy early on. “I had this sense of boys having more freedom than girls. Later, as a postgraduate student in LA, she swung hard in the opposite direction with frills, dresses and hyperfemininity before realising it wasn’t her. “Eventually, I settled into a place where it’s not masculine, it’s not feminine. It’s somewhere in the middle. That feels better.” In high school, a senior once warned her, “You dress like a boy. You should know that men are not attracted to that.” The comment lodged itself somewhere in her brain. Years later, when she started dating her now husband, she briefly tried to course-correct. “I went shopping and bought this grey frilly dress. I don’t think I wore it more than once. I was like, OK, I cannot do this. It’s just not me.” “I do think overall he is very secure in his masculinity and who he is,” she says. “So he doesn’t feel like his wife has to be feminine or look feminine to project a certain kind of image.” It helps that he’s a designer. “If he likes something, he’ll just say, ‘Oh wow, that looks cool, babe.’ It’s not limited to any specific kind of outfit. He sees the colour composition, the shapes.” In other words, he has taste. Marcella echoes that dynamic. “He absolutely loves it,” they say of their partner’s reaction to their personal style. “He’s very fashion-forward himself and it’s been great because we get to share closets.” Which, quite frankly, is the final frontier of any relationship. I see it in my own relationship, too. I’ll show my boyfriend pieces I’m considering buying and genuinely take his opinion on my outfits into account, which, to my perpetual shock, often improve the look. He runs his clothes by me, loves going shopping together, sends me reels of clothes he thinks I'll like and always has a new pair of Of course, not all responses are enlightened. Gaur points out that when she receives hate from men, it often stems from discomfort. “It can be threatening to see a woman showing up in a powerful way. Because in those minds, masculinity equals power. Men expect women to dress a certain way because I think they’re explicitly looking for softness, which to them is weakness.” Which brings us back to the original question: are men evolving? Maybe some are. Maybe the male gaze is splintering. Maybe there’s a growing cohort of men who find autonomy attractive, who are secure in their own masculinity and their femininity. They understand design, appreciate shape and proportion and find any well-put-together outfit as compelling as a body-con gown. Or maybe, it’s just really hot when a woman dresses like a man.

The skirt’s versatile design allows it to be tied up in multiple ways, ensuring a flattering look for all body types,” says Advait. What catches your eye the most is its painterly print. “Sweeping brushstroke forms in crimson, deep terracotta and burnt sienna cut across an ivory cotton satin base, lending the look an artful edge. The composition channels the raw energy of Abstract Expressionism and yet remains wearable. The idea was to imagine strokes that are gestural and spontaneous, as though the cotton satin fabric itself was laid flat and painted by hand in a single, fluid motion,” the designer shares. The print did not originate digitally. “It was first born on paper, drawn entirely by hand before being translated onto fabric. Each brushstroke you see is a deliberate mark made by a human hand, later rendered onto the cloth to preserve every raw, imperfect edge of the original artwork.”

article_title: Sonam Kapoor’s lime Shehlaa Khan ensemble reworked Mughal florals in paint and zardozi
sub_title: Rhea Kapoor styled the look with layers of jewellery
article_content: In February 2026, Sonam Ahuja Kapoor celebrated her second pregnancy with a godh bharai ceremony, hosted by her family. For the occasion, the mother-to-be opted for a bespoke outfit by friend and designer Shehlaa Khan. The lime look was conceived in close collaboration with Kapoor’s sister and stylist Rhea Kapoor. “We wanted to do something special and still use a signature style of my label,” Khan shares. What they arrived at was a silhouette that is thoughtful and comfortable, featuring a bubble skirt, a contoured blouse and a flowing kimono cape, defined by a classic Indian-style dupatta. “Given that it's an Indian godh bharai, the only thing contemporary about the outfit was its silhouette,” explains Khan. Despite that deliberate modernity of form, the overall impression is traditional. On Kapoor, the structure of the blouse and the volume of the bubble skirt introduced a sculptural quality, whereas the kimono cape softened the look with fluid movement. The starting point for the look’s embellishment was unambiguous in its ambition. “The idea was to resemble a Mughal style painting, and therefore we used the signature hand-painting technique as the base of the embellishment on a Chanderi silk fabric. which is rich yet represents a vintage Indian aesthetic.” Mughal miniature painting, which flourished as a courtly artform between the 16th and 18th centuries, is defined by vibrant mineral pigments and an obvious synthesis of Indian, Persian and European influences. The paintings are celebrated for their realistic portraiture and naturalistic depictions of flora and fauna, and this is the exact visual language that Khan has translated onto fabric. The hand-painted crimson blossoms and brushed-gold leaves were elevated through zardozi embroidery worked in nakshi and saadi materials. “The festive nature of the event required some sparkles, to give the look of Zari work used in extensive garments of women from royalty in the Mughal era," Khan adds. “The outfit was a very intricate yet heartfelt tribute to the relationship Sonam holds with the brand since its early years," adds Khan. “It took a long time and several hours of handwork of various artisans to bring this outfit together.” Colour, too, Khan says, played a defining role in shaping the mood. “We chose lime because Sonam loves green but yet wanted it to be a bright and a happy shade for the joyous occasion.” Rhea styled her look with jewellery that blended heirloom sentiment with artisanal charm. The necklace and earrings were from Kapoor’s personal collection, while the ring and gucha came from Amrapali Jewels, the hathphool, waist belt and pearl kadas from Sheetal Zaveri, and additional kadas from Maalka By Varun Haria and Falguni Mehta.

article_title: Why are Indian weddings with dancing gorillas going viral?
sub_title: There was a time when the best hope for an Indian wedding to become Instagram-famous was to look like a Pinterest moodboard. But as the rules of virality change, so are desi weddings
article_content: At 11:30 pm, Vishesh Anand and Kavisha Chawla’s cocktail party was winding down. Their guests were at the finish line of a marathon March wedding in An Indore-based jeweller, Anand is referring to the dancing-gorilla trend. First In Delhi’s Sultanpuri, Manoj Kumar’s mascot entertainment company, Gori Boy Events, has become the poster boy (or gorilla) of this trend. “The DJ happened to play ‘Laila Mein Laila’ at a wedding we had booked in February, and my employee in a gorilla suit gave a power-packed performance. I filmed a video of him dancing and added my contact number when I posted it online. In 24 hours, I got a million views,” Kumar says proudly. Today, that “It’s been on everyone’s feed. Anyone planning an occasion is getting tagged by their friends in comments saying, ‘If the gorilla is not coming, I’m not coming,’” says Ayushi Gupta, a community manager at When Anand’s wedding planners failed to find a gorilla performer, he went so far as to take matters into his own hands. “It was two days before the wedding. I thought, ‘How can we not get the gorilla?’ So I searched and booked it myself,” he says. In fact, Anand took it a notch higher, hiring a panda as well. “People were going gaga over them. Even if Amitabh Bachchan was at our wedding, they wouldn’t have danced with him as much as they did with the animals,” says his wife. The gorilla, though entertaining, is a symptom of a growing obsession with online visibility. “Many times, people come to us saying, ‘The goal is to go Vikram Mehta, founder and executive director of wedding planning company MPire Events, adds that peer pressure is a major driver for wedding virality. “People care about what their social circuits think, and there’s a lot of competition within them,” he explains, confessing that he planned a padel-themed wedding brunch when racquet sports exploded in popularity a few years ago. Everyone wants a gorilla but does anyone care about what the gorilla wants? “The performers feel very hot in the suit but no one asks about our well-being. People will book us and come up to compliment us but won’t offer food or water,” says Kumar, who ensures his performers rest for 30 minutes for every one hour of dancing. “He looked too young to be in that huge gorilla costume,” Gupta confesses, estimating that the performer could not have been older than 20. “He’s just trying to earn a living and we’re paying him, but it’s not enough.” For Kumar too, virality has cost him his sleep—people call him incessantly, often late into the night, with requests to hire the gorilla to drink or sleep with them, even offering two lakhs to buy the suit and the performer in it. Despite the hassle, he knows the novelty of his character will likely wear off in two years. And then the next big thing will come along.

I’d step into my mum’s Now, twenty years later, the occasions to wear a tiara are few and far between, but there is one moment I know I can count on: my wedding. The Indian bride, after all, is something of a real-life princess. And on the day that marks the beginning of her happily ever after, she certainly knows how to look the part. “ Of course, extravagance has never been unfamiliar territory for the Indian wedding. The lehengas get heavier every year, the diamonds get bigger and the guest list is often comparable to a small village. In that context, the tiara feels like a natural evolution. But once the wedding diary closes, how do you justify a piece of jewellery, however beautiful, for a single day? The good news is that the tiara is far more versatile than it first appears. “It isn’t frozen in one format. A central stone can be detached and worn as a pendant or elements can be reimagined as So, if you're considering a tiara on your wedding day (as you should), “the starting point has to be the stone. Every creation really begins there,” adds Lodha. Take Alok Lodha’s Firdaus Tiara, which draws from the Mughal sarpech. Vintage mine-cut diamonds set in a Victorian tarnished black finish form scrolling arabesques, framing the central stone, a 28-carat Colombian emerald. A plume of white feathers adds a lightness to the piece. Here, the As children, a tiara allows us to indulge in fantasy, a small sparkling promise that we might one day step into a fairytale of our own. As adults, it becomes a piece of jewellery shaped by craftsmanship, history and taste. While it may make its grandest appearance on a wedding day, the tiara was never really meant for just one moment. It’s designed to evolve, to be reimagined, and, if you’re lucky, to be passed down. After all, every princess deserves a crown.

article_title: Is the intimate desi wedding replacing the big, fat Indian wedding?
sub_title: The real luxury at an Indian wedding isn’t scale, but time
article_content: A typical Indian wedding conjures up images of a beautifully decorated stage, the bride and groom at its centre, vowing to spend the rest of their lives together. Beyond them, a sea of people watching. Including the bride’s uncle’s new astrologer and the best man’s breakdancing troupe from college. But for some couples, the tides are shifting, stars are realigning and the guest list is dwindling. An intimate desi wedding sounds faintly contradictory, and yet, it has snuck up on us. Lists that used to run well into the hundreds are now tapering off in the fifties and, gasp... even twenties. Why are couples going down this lean route? Or rather, how are they getting away with it? According to Krish Sheth and Shefali Sharma, whose 55-­person wedding took place in Rishikesh, the trick is simple: make sure your But the couple didn’t begin with a number in mind. After months of searching, they found a property that felt right, Anand Kashi by the Ganges. It had the warm energy they were looking for and, more importantly, a limited capacity. So, the venue wrote the guest list. Years of attending large weddings had already planted the seed. “It’s like an attendance register,” Sheth says. “You show up, say hello, pose for a photo and move on.” Anyone they didn’t have at least three core memories with, didn’t make their list. For those working behind-the-scenes, this shift has been a pleasant change of pace. The pandemic was certainly a catalyst—proof that ceremonies could still feel complete without being excessive. Wedding planner Priya Maganti of RVR Eventz & Design, who recently hosted around 180 guests—intimate by her standards—knew every guest there by name. “By the end, people didn’t know if I was the planner or part of the family,” she laughs. That closeness changes everything. With fewer guests, you actually get to host, to make sure people have eaten well and to be present. But Indian Shlok Punjabi and Katyayni Gupta, who hosted a 20-person wedding, recall long conversations with their highly social parents who struggled with the absence of old friends and extended family. What helped was that family involvement started long before the wedding. “The proposal wasn’t something we did alone,” shares Punjabi. “Her brother, her mom, my parents, my And those conversations were well worth it. For three days in Tulum, Mexico, the small group talked endlessly, danced together and simply existed in the same space. “You just can’t manufacture that feeling of togetherness with a larger group,” adds Gupta. It translates on-camera too, documented for years to come. “You can hear more—small chatter, half sentences, private jokes,” shares photographer Siddharth Sharma of House on the Clouds, “It changes the way moments unfold behind the lens.” With fewer moving parts, you notice details that usually get lost. For Herit Vachhani and Kinjal Patel, the decision to go small came from fatigue. Midway through planning a large-scale wedding, Patel realised the process itself had drained the joy out of the idea. “It wasn’t fun for us. For an entire year, this was all we talked about.” Her 300-person engagement party had already given her a preview. “You can’t really enjoy the day because you’re thinking: what if someone spills wine on the floor or what if someone breaks a vase.” Their eventual wedding by Lake Como had just nine guests. While intimate weddings are often framed as emotional decisions rather than financial ones, they are considerably easier on the bank account. Fewer guests mean less logistics and more freedom to spend intentionally. “There’s space to be more mindful,” shares experience designer Eeshaan Kashyap, of Eeshaan Kashyap & Co and Tablescape by Eeshaan, “We had a bride who wanted to drape her old The big Indian wedding isn’t going anywhere. There is no substitute for the collective joy it brings. But alongside it, there is room for another version. What you lose in fireworks, you gain in time—the rarest luxury. Time to sit with your parents without being pulled away. Time to eat with your friends instead of waving at them across a room. Time to finish conversations, to linger after they’re over and to celebrate the beginning of a new life.

article_title: When it comes to wedding jewellery, why should women have all the fun?
sub_title: It’s the groom’s time to shine, literally
article_content: At a time when Indian weddings are only getting grander, Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna's wedding offered a masterclass in wedding jewellery for men. For their Telugu ceremony at ITC Mementos, Udaipur, he wore layered gold temple pieces crafted by Shree Jewellers: a kasu mala stacked with a long haram, cuffs, bajuband, earrings and a broad oddiyanam belt cinching his dhoti. Elephant and tiger motifs, deep nakshi engraving and traditional silhouettes drawn from heritage, the unapologetic layering and head-to-toe commitment pushed the look beyond accessorising into a ceremonial ensemble. When it comes to wedding jewellery, brides have seemingly endless options. So to say, wedding jewellery for men should no longer be an afterthought. “Grooms today are becoming far more experimental and expressive with their jewellery. They are moving beyond the traditional strings of pearls and embracing statement pieces that reflect their personality, be it with a handcrafted kalgi, gemstone buttons or heirloom brooches,” says Sunita Shekhawat, founder and CEO of Sunita Shekhawat. Below, India’s leading jewellery designers get into some classic, other new-age and a few modular jewels for the modern-day groom. Chokers are no longer just the bride’s territory. Grooms are now styling chokers with long necklaces and even ranihaars that elevate their look by many folds. Extra points for colourblocking. Think kanthas, whether monotone or multicoloured, in tumbles of emerald, rubies and other precious gemstones that can be paired with polki chokers. Jadau kamarbandhs are having a moment. Although a tad out there, when it comes to wedding jewellery for men, grooms are styling them on sherwanis to tie up the look. It is a multifunctional piece that can later be used as a necklace by both the bride and the groom. Brooches today come in a wide range of themes, from animal motifs and floral-inspired designs to sleek geometric forms. Polki and jadau brooches featuring striking centre gemstones such as classic rubies and emeralds, as well as playful, vivid stones like lapis and tourmaline, sit really well on neutral-toned sherwanis. They also transition seamlessly into modern wardrobes, making them heirlooms worth investing in. Think beyond the watch. Layer bracelets or kada sets that blend gold with gemstones. It adds a regal touch without feeling overdone. A signet ring is timeless; it carries a strong sense of identity and legacy when customised, engraved with initials, a family crest or studded with a gemstone that resonates with the wearer. It’s a piece that truly becomes a part of you and easily transcends into your occasionwear wardrobe. Choose one statement piece and build around it. For instance, if you’re wearing a heavy necklace, go lighter on the brooch and buttons. Also, make sure your jewellery complements your outfit’s tone–gold for warmer hues and silver or platinum for cooler shades. A strand of pearls has remained a mainstay in many a bijoux box and for good reason. It is regal, gender-neutral and elegant. Even a string of uncut diamonds works wonders on both neutral and jewel-toned outfits. When they say the devil is in the details, they’re talking about gemstone buttons. Vintage-inspired sherwani buttons encrusted with gemstones of choice make for a regal addition to the groom’s look. While emerald buttons usually take the centre stage, ones with meenakari (coloured enamelling) are also being favoured now. Trust polki cufflinks featuring uncut diamonds or enamel detailing to add a subtle yet regal touch to the groom’s ensemble. Get them engraved with the groom’s initials to make for a bespoke accessory. Pieces that can be detached, adjusted and layered to fit multiple occasions offer versatility that’s second to none. A polki necklace that can be worn as a single statement strand or in layers is a gift that keeps giving. Similarly, sherwani buttons that can be transformed into cufflinks for a more pared-down look for the post-wedding events are ingenious ways to make the most of your jewels. Complement the bride’s jewels and apparel tones without replicating them. And what of the groom’s own fit? Lighter pastels pair beautifully with emeralds and Polki, while deeper hues shine with uncut diamonds or sapphires.

article_content: In an era where Indian weddings have grown synonymous with extravagance, Rashmika Mandanna and Vijay Deverakonda’s wedding was a refreshing reminder that the essence of a wedding still lies in tradition. For all the crystal chandeliers and sparkling fireworks, nothing quite compares to centuries-old customs that are carried and worn with pride. Between the layers of gold temple jewellery and the couple's traditional ensemble, the wedding felt like a page straight out of Indian mythology. Set at ITC Mementos, Udaipur, the morning honoured Deverakonda’s Telugu traditions, while the evening paid homage to Mandanna’s Kodava roots from Coorg. Kodava weddings are known for being intimate and community-led, placing ancestry, nature and family blessings at the heart of the ceremony. The bride traditionally wears a rich silk For the ceremony, Mandanna opted for a rust silk sari with a bold-red border, custom-made by His gold pieces, crafted by Shree Jewellers, featured layered haars, cuffs, bajuband, earrings, anklet and a broad oddiyanam belt that cinched the dhoti. Elephant motifs symbolised wisdom, tiger elements agility and deep nakshi engraving gave each piece dimension. He also wore two heavy necklaces—a kasu mala and a long haram. Mandanna wore temple Small rituals added layers of meaning throughout, like Mandanna's bridal entry with the coconut in her hand. Known as kobbari bondam, the tender coconut is carried as a symbol of prosperity, purity and fertility. Black dishti chukka dots were applied on both their cheeks during the mangala snanam or holy bath, to ward off the evil eye as they stepped into married life. Mandanna wore minimal mehendi, while Deverakonda applied alta to his hands and feet during his pelli koduku ceremony. On their foreheads, both wore basikam—a gold ornament tied with turmeric-laced thread—along with matching pelli bottu tilaks, symbolising their transition into a new life together. A curtain (addutera) separated them until the jeelakarra bellam ceremony, where they placed a paste of cumin and jaggery on each other’s heads. The ritual signifies unity, balance and the hope that their marriage, like the mixture itself, remains inseparable. The entire celebration, thoughtfully planned and designed by RVR Eventz Design, brought these rituals to life with a setting that enhanced heritage rather than overshadowing it. At a time when everyone is obsessed with what’s new, Mandanna and Deverakonda chose to foreground their roots, proving tradition doesn't always have to be the opposite of modernity.

sub_title: We asked the jewellery pros to give us the inside scoop on how to safely clean a diamond ring at home
article_content: Notice your engagement ring is losing its shine? It’s not damaged; you just need to give it a refresh. Luckily, learning how to clean a “Cleaning your ring at home is a great way to maintain its sparkle,” says Lauren Grunstein, vice president of Want to learn how to do a DIY clean that will actually make a major difference? Ahead, we ask jewellery pros to give us the inside scoop on how to clean a diamond ring at home. Another ring cleaning method to follow is similar to the one above, yet you replace the soap with a window cleaning solution, like Colin. Grunstein advises using a solution that's three parts water and one part cleaner to get the best cleaning formula. A final alternative is to create a solution that mixes one part rubbing alcohol with three parts warm water. This method allows you to soak your ring for a shorter time period. Just 10 minutes should do the trick. You can also purchase jewellery cleaning solutions that can safely clean your ring in a pinch. “I believe the easiest option is to use products you already have at home, like dish soap and rubbing alcohol," says Grunstein. “While diamonds are the hardest naturally occurring substance on Earth and fine jewellery is crafted for everyday wear, it’s important to remember that it’s not indestructible,” shares Kothari. “A common misconception is that jewellery can handle anything.” That means you should take special care of your engagement ring, especially when giving it extra attention while cleaning. “To avoid damaging your precious piece, common mistakes to steer clear of [include] using harsh chemicals like bleach or household cleaners—these can damage both the metal and the diamond,” says Kothari. “Scrubbing too aggressively with a stiff brush can loosen prongs, dislodge pavé-set diamonds, or scratch the metal,” recommends Kothari. The jeweller also advises never cleaning over an open sink. “Always make sure you're in a secure spot to prevent your ring from slipping down the drain,” she says. If your ring includes While gold and platinum can easily follow the soap-and-water cleaning method, a silver band should be handled differently. “You can restore its luster using at-home remedies like a mixture of vinegar and baking soda or an at-home silver polishing kit,” says Grunstein. A deep clean of your ring isn’t always necessary. There are other solutions you can do in a pinch. “I keep a simple plastic Tupperware, a soft toothbrush, and a mini bottle of Dawn dish soap under my sink. If I forget to steam or ultrasonic clean my jewelry at work and want my pieces to not just sparkle but really glisten, I add a drop of soap and some warm water and let the jewelry soak while I do my morning routine,” says Trau. “Then, I give it a gentle brush and rinse it before putting it on.” She adds, “One important tip is to make sure your rings are completely dry before wearing them to avoid irritation.” Just like you go for an annual checkup at the doctor, it’s recommended to take your engagement ring to a professional jeweller once a year to clean and check on the condition of the piece. “A professional cleaning will make your ring look brand new (there’s nothing quite like it!), and the jeweller can check for any loose stones or needed repairs,” says Grunstein. “Additionally, we encourage our clients to stop by for a cleaning anytime they’re in the neighborhood, everyone feels so much better with sparkling jewellery.” Kothari adds, if you ever feel like your stone is rattling in the setting, you should visit as well: “That’s a sign it’s loose and needs immediate attention to avoid losing it.”

article_title: Inside real weddings: A photographer’s guide to capturing intimate celebrations
sub_title: From shared laughter to candid, intimate moments, Fourfold Pictures brings every wedding emotion to life behind the lens
article_content: Couples are reclaiming their wedding stories and prioritising emotion and authenticity over perfection. Rather than putting on a spectacle, the focus is on intimate and meaningful interactions with loved ones, with photographs becoming the ultimate keepsakes. That’s why picking the right wedding photographer is an essential part of planning your big day. Mumbai-based wedding photographer duo Gaurav and Priyanka Shukla came together to capture candid memories. Co-founders of Fourfold Pictures, they have a knack for anticipating pivotal moments, with honesty in storytelling being paramount to their work. Over time, Gaurav and Priyanka have built a brand that attracts couples seeking intention, aesthetic depth, and a distinct visual identity. Notably, A-listers such as actors Parineeti Chopra and Aadar Jain, singer Prakriti Kakar, and content creator Aaliyah Kashyap, among others, are part of their repertoire. While editorial sophistication defines their portfolio, the heart of Fourfold Pictures is rooted in human connection. From intimate ceremonies to grand celebrations, the brand is dedicated to creating enduring visual stories—memories couples can revisit for years to come. The photographers share their insights on capturing intimate nuptials, understanding what modern couples value most, and remembering what truly matters once the camera starts rolling. “We begin by understanding emotion before aesthetics,” says the duo. Every wedding starts with an internal mood board—light, texture, rhythm, restraint. The final gallery is edited with a fashion sensibility and a storyteller’s heart: timeless, not trend-led. Intimate weddings allow for emotional closeness. With fewer people, the energy shifts inward. The focus shifts from spectacle to presence, nuance, and genuine human connection. Each wedding has its own visual language. Sometimes the destination exists as a subtle backdrop; other times it becomes a character within the story. “We let the location influence colour, light, and mood—never overpowering the couple themselves,” mentions the duo. Intimacy creates space for stillness. “We look for the moments in between moments—glances, silences, and gentle gestures. Those details often carry the deepest emotion,” the duo reflects. Trust comes with intention and discretion. “We work unobtrusively, allowing couples to remain fully present. When they feel unobserved, authenticity emerges naturally,” shares the duo. Culture shapes rhythm and expression. “We respond by adapting my pace and framing—honouring tradition while maintaining an editorial lens that feels contemporary and refined,” says the duo. Think beyond simply capturing moments. Focus on how you want the day to feel. When emotion leads, the images naturally become aesthetically meaningful. Intimate weddings are often mistaken for being simpler, but in reality, they’re emotionally layered and visually sophisticated. They allow for more intentional storytelling, editorial-style portraits, and visionary experiences that are often harder to achieve in larger celebrations. “A quiet pause shared between the couple, away from the ceremony and guests. No performance—just presence. These are the moments that linger long after the wedding ends,” Gaurav concludes.

In that case, weigh your options. Perhaps placing more of an emphasis on size and less on colour and clarity is worth considering. They want a ring that feels ‘fashion’ and relevant, but also timeless—not basic, boring, or predictable," Azlee designer Baylee Zwart says. "They come to us for a ring that’s unusual but still clean and sleek so it won’t go out of One route is a colourful, non-diamond centre stone. “Historically, colored gemstones were actually the original choice for engagement rings,” Moross shares, nodding to “Custom feels more special than just walking into a store and picking something,” Hannah explains. “Generally speaking, a lot of people now want something that walks the line between vintage and modern. It’s not so much about a big diamond anymore—they want quality over size, or a unique shape, like a rose cut. And a lot of people are ditching diamonds altogether. Pierce’s brand draws inspiration from poesy rings, a style of ring that dates back to medieval times, which were bands with inscriptions on the inside—secret messages of love and devotion. Pierce has designed rings with engravings of letters, monograms, phrases in a loved one’s handwriting, and more. “Engraving is a really seamless way of marking [the ring] with your own story,” she says. Plus, hand-engraving seems to be having a moment (see: Traditionally, fiancèes receive an engagement ring at the Engagement ring shopping can be a daunting task—get by with a little help from your friends. Ask those who’ve gotten engaged for jeweller recommendations and call upon someone who knows you and your future spouse and whose taste you respect. Worst-case scenario, if your intended hates what you’ve come up with, you should be able to exchange it for something else. You want your future spouse to love both you and the jewellery you buy forever. No one likes to think about the possibility of losing such a meaningful piece of jewellery, but sometimes it’s inevitable. Engagement ring insurance is exactly what it sounds like: financial protection that can cover replacement, repairs, or cost reimbursement for your ring. Although it’s not the most romantic aspect of this process, it’s equally vital to consider. During the Depression, in a campaign that would’ve made Don Draper proud, De Beers’s advertising geniuses started running an ad pushing men to spend one month’s salary on a ring if they wanted to be “responsible.” By the 1980s, it jumped up to two months. These days, the rule of thumb that’s often referenced is that one should fork over at least three months’ salary when purchasing this piece of forever jewellery. This should be nothing like that—this is no procrastinator’s endeavour. Finding or creating the perfect engagement ring means putting a lot of time into the process. Every step takes care and consideration—and while you want your fiancée to adore her ring, you want to make sure you aren’t rushed along the way.

article_title: This Delhi couple’s story is the perfect example of the invisible string theory
sub_title: How Pavani Nagpal and Karan Chhabra’s parallel lives, chance meeting and artistic wedding came together in a story of serendipity
article_content: Fate works in mysterious ways, bringing together two people who are meant to be with each other. East Asian folklore refers to this phenomenon as the ‘red thread of fate’ or, as popular culture describes it, the invisible string theory. A large part of content today, from books to movies, is inspired by this whimsical bit of folklore. It depicts two people crossing paths through time and distance, never quite pausing, until one destined moment of clarity (a meet-cute, for all you rom-com enthusiasts) brings them together. Bringing this fictional belief to life is the story of Pavani Nagpal and Karan Chhabra. Nagpal, a visual artist, and Chhabra, a tech professional, studied in the same school and later also went to the same university, walking the corridors and complaining about their teachers. But their paths never crossed. Years passed and Nagpal founded her own art studio, Pavsarts Art Studio, while Chhabra became the CEO of Acefone, a business communications company. Until they finally met in what would seem like a scene right out of a romantic movie, at a party, where Nagpal accidentally spilled a drink on Chhabra. Chhabra, like the ever-charming male lead, joked that he deserved a discount on one of Nagpal’s paintings. “And that single moment changed everything,” the visual artist tells us. Fate had set the dice rolling. The couple began dating, got engaged and were married, all within a year. Their wedding celebrations were a blend of art, heritage, couture and the magic of two people finding their way to each other. Unfolding slowly over a month, each celebration reflected a different emotion, from devotion to joy. Starting the wedding ceremonies on an auspicious note, the couple organised a mata ki chowki. Bathed in shades of red and enhanced by two of the bride’s paintings, the decor made the space look like a film set. Matching the Indian classical sensibilities, the bride wore a Sabyasachi ensemble while the groom adorned a custom lakhnawi kurta set. A few weeks after that, the pair got engaged in a joyous ceremony filled with song, dance and laughter. The venue was decorated elegantly, inspired by a painting Nagpal had made just before meeting Chhabra. “My painting manifested him in my life,” the bride exclaimed. She donned another beautiful Sabyasachi outfit for the ceremony while the groom complemented her in a timeless Rohit Bal outfit. The mehendi was a deeply personal affair for Nagpal, as she hosted it at Pavsarts Art Studio, her own space, surrounded by colours, canvases and her work. “It felt like my journey as an artist and my journey in love were coming together in the same space,” she said. Wearing Anamika Khanna and Manish Malhotra, the bride and groom fit into the venue just right, looking like they’d walked straight out of one of Nagpal’s paintings. The mehendi night was followed by a floral haldi morning at The Leela Palace, Chanakyapuri. The couple and their wedding guests played phoolon ki haldi, a ritual where, along with the traditional turmeric, fragrant flowers are also used. A highlight of the event was when the usually calm and composed Chhabra surprised everyone with an energetic performance. The bride looked radiant in a bright pink Shobhika Bhandari saree while the groom matched her, wearing a pastel pink Rohit Bal ensemble. The bright and cold morning of November eight marked the couple’s wedding day. It was a traditional and emotional celebration, less about spectacle and more about the couple beginning their new life together. In royal Sabyasachi and Rohit Bal ensembles, the couple looked radiant with happiness and love, surrounded by near and dear ones. What began as parallel lives eventually became a shared one, guided by timing, chance and perhaps a little bit of destiny. Two people, once strangers walking the same corridors, were unknowingly tethered by an invisible string, until fate finally pulled them together into a moment and led them to a lifetime of companionship.

article_title: “I wear it on my middle finger”: Inside the booming market for divorce rings
sub_title: “I’m complimented on it surprisingly often, which always makes me smile. Not because of what it represents to anyone else, but because it reminds me that I trusted myself when it mattered"
article_content: Peer through the window of Annoushka Ducas’s London boutique in the evening, and you might spy women poring over diamonds and sipping champagne. But they aren’t congregating to peruse engagement rings or push presents, they’re toasting the signing of Ducas is just one of a host of jewellers responding to the growing appetite for divorce rings, fuelled in part by the sizeable jewels sported by A-listers after they’ve signed on the dotted line to singledom. Take Emily Ratajkowski, who back in March 2024, commemorated her divorce from her husband of two years, Sebastian Bear-McClard, with two platinum and 18-carat rings designed by Alison Lou, which incorporated the pear-shaped and princess-cut diamonds from her In January, original power stylist and newly inaugurated Real Housewife Rachel Zoe marked her split from her husband of over 20 years, Rodger Berman, with a jaw-dropping three-stone divorce ring designed by Ring Concierge, which transformed the huge cushion-cut diamond of her halo engagement ring. Elsewhere, celebrity dermatologist Barbara Sturm commissioned her Jessica McCormack divorce ring before her separation from husband Adam Waldman had even been finalised. “Once you’ve made the decision, you’re already there, even if the paperwork isn’t through,” she says. Posting the final creation on Instagram in October 2025–a chunky twisted gold ring with a pear-shaped diamond–she namechecked EmRata as her inspiration. Unsurprisingly, East London jeweller Rachel Boston–who says she has been working on divorce ring commissions for the last four years–has found her clients clamouring for bespoke designs that look anything but traditionally “bridal”. “Clients are gravitating towards pieces that feel more grounded and everyday, like chunky bands, sculptural settings, and designs that can be worn as part of a daily uniform,” she explains. “Signet style rings and wide gold bands are popular.” Chelsea-based jeweller Jessie Thomas agrees. “We see a lot of chunky yellow and white gold pieces, with heavy settings and large stones.” Tania and Dima Nawbar, of fourth-generation Beirut-based jeweller Atelier Nawbar, also note the same affinity for the oversized. A recent divorce ring commission saw the central diamond and halo stones from a wedding and engagement ring transformed into a pebble-like cocktail ring, shimmering with bezel-set diamonds. “I hadn’t expected how often I’d absently reach for my wedding rings without thinking, or how their absence would become an unwanted reminder of the struggle I was going through,” says 32-year-old Madeleine Phillips. The East Sussex-based marketing director commissioned a divorce ring three months after her separation was finalised. “I didn’t want to repurpose my wedding or engagement rings. At that point they felt too emotionally loaded, and looking back, I’m glad I didn’t try and bring a piece of my past into the present. I wanted something symbolic, that felt very intentional, but it needed to be new.” Working with an online jeweller, Phillips commissioned a yellow gold ring set with baguette-cut “deliberately defiant” black diamonds. “It has 11 stones, one for each year we were together. That wasn’t something I set out to do, but once I saw it, the choice felt precise, rather than sentimental.” Phillips initially wore her divorce ring on her ring finger, before having it resized to fit her middle one. “That progression was always part of the plan I had for it, and the way the ring has evolved with me feels part of its story.” Lylie’s Eliza Walters has also noted commissions for rings designed to be worn on the middle finger, like chunky Etruscan-inspired settings, “intentionally removing any visual or symbolic association with a traditional engagement ring”. Barbara Sturm also designed her ring to sit on the middle of her hand. “But my 11-year-old daughter, Pepper, told me it looked cooler on my index finger,” she says, smiling. Twice-divorced Victoria Comstock-Kershaw, an art critic, continues to wear both of her engagement rings stacked on her ring finger. “I’ve kept wearing after the divorce, which I’m told is absolutely insane, but my logic was: I liked them enough at the time, and I continue to trust my taste in jewellery more than I trust my taste in men,” she says. At her weddings, the 27-year-old had exchanged vows with rings she already owned: choosing first a green tourmaline and silver ring gifted to her by her grandmother, and then a diamond and lilac sapphire band from a now-defunct jeweller in Burlington Arcade that was originally a 21st birthday present to her mother, who gave it to her daughter when she turned 21. “Aesthetically I find them immensely satisfying (I often get my nails done to match the first one),” she says. “Socially, they are simultaneously a good deterrent to flash at flirters (‘sorry, married!’) and a great conversation starter with anybody who compliments them (‘what do you mean your It doesn’t have to be a ring, either. Barbara Sturm repurposed two small pear-shaped diamonds from her original engagement ring into earrings, while Annoushka and Rachel Boston have had enquiries into pendant necklaces. “Divorce has a way of unsettling your sense of self. Change was going to be uncomfortable regardless, so I chose to mark it on my own terms, with a reminder of the version of me who chose decisiveness over doubt, at a point when that really mattered,” says Phillips. “Now, my ring feels more about confidence than recovery. I’m complimented on it surprisingly often, which always makes me smile. Not because of what it represents to anyone else, but because it reminds me that I trusted myself when it mattered.”
