article_title: Colleagues to coupledom: How this couple went from co-workers to wedding vows without a kerfuffle
sub_title: Andrea Kurunathan and Prem Anand Umapathy share a business, workplace and most waking hours. Here’s how planning their wedding revealed why they work so well together
article_content: For Andrea Kurunathan and Prem Anand Umapathy, love was never rushed. It unfolded slowly, shaped by friendship, shared ambition, humour and years of perseverance. Kurunathan, an aesthetic physician, and Umapathy, a civil engineer and interior designer, met through mutual friends when they were 18 and 22. They were polar opposites, and their first impressions of each other weren’t promising—no one would have guessed that the couple would go on to run a successful business together, let alone turn that partnership into a marriage that began with exchanging vows by the sea in Phuket. So how did the couple find themselves in a South Indian wedding in Thailand? Through years of friendship—supporting one another through educational endeavours, career uncertainty and major life decisions—Kurunathan fell for Umapathy’s humour and calm steadiness, while Umapathy admired her drive and clarity. Before tying the knot, the pair built a life together, navigating pressure, differences and ambition. They co-founded Luxury Derm Clinic, a luxury aesthetic clinic in Chennai, learning each other’s rhythms and accepting that being opposites did not mean being incompatible. So when it came time to plan a multi-city, deeply personal wedding, they approached it the same way they approach everything else: with intention, defined roles and very little ego. Here’s how they did it while enjoying the process of planning a wedding instead of letting it stress them out. One of the most important reasons the couple work well together is their existing partnership. It made the process of planning the wedding easier—they already knew how decisions were made, who would lead where, and when to step back. “We approached the wedding the same way we approach building our business. We have always known that we are better together than alone, and that belief shapes everything we build,” shared the bride. “We divided responsibilities instinctively, based on what each of us enjoys and does best,” Umapathy explained. The bride took charge of the aesthetics, storytelling and creative direction, while the groom supported her vision through precise execution, drawing on his technical expertise. From a floral mehendi sundowner to a traditional South Indian wedding in Phuket, (a location deeply personal to the couple) every ceremony was Kurunathan’s brainchild, brought to life through Umapathy’s engineering precision. For two people so different in temperament, disagreements were inevitable, but they rarely turned personal. “We understand each other’s strengths and give each other a lot of space. We do not step into each other’s territory unless help is needed. When it is, we show up fully. That balance is what keeps things easy between us,” said Kurunathan. There were no major disagreements, only a few light-hearted ones. Kurunathan wanted to be the loud, proud Indian bride with elaborate outfits and wedding dances, while the shy and reserved Umapathy wasn’t comfortable with all the attention. In the end, the groom surprised everyone on the dance floor and delivered a wedding speech that had guests in stitches. Kurunathan’s looks—from a blue floral Ariyali lehenga by Mrunalini Rao at the mehendi to a classic red-and-gold Kanchipuram silk saree for the wedding—were striking designer outfits. On the other hand, Umapathy chose refined, understated ensembles, staying true to himself while still complementing the bride. After watching the couple build a successful business together, their families trusted their clarity and vision. While family members played a central role in shaping the wedding, final decisions always rested with the bride and groom. “Everyone respected each other’s space, and we were all more focused on fine-tuning and shaping ideas rather than controlling them. It became a very collaborative process. It was not a wedding run for us; it was a wedding built by us, with family standing firmly behind us,” the groom explained. In the end, it’s about knowing whose vision to trust, building something together, and leaving ego out of the equation. And that, perhaps, is what made the Kurunathan-Umapathy wedding truly special.

article_title: 4 almost-brides tell us how they braved wedding season in India after their weddings were called off
sub_title: Spill the tea, but don’t be tacky
article_content: Congratulations to us all. We’re halfway through wedding season in India. We’ve braved nuptials we were invited to and reluctantly attended, as well as those we watched unfold on But, let’s admit it, the most You know the ones: the blended WhatsApp wedding group suddenly goes eerily silent. Soon enough, private chats are ablaze with gleeful/glum I-knew-its, followed by Now imagine being the unwilling heroine perched at the centre of the expensive operatic mess that is a cancelled wedding. Or its polite cousin, the indefinitely impending nuptials. And imagine enduring a These four women survived the carnage to give us a definitive ‘how to’ guide: how to prep for the chaos, how to commiserate without being cloying, how to be a girl’s girl even while dishing the dirt. It’s going to hurt to see people get married on or around your wedding day, even if you’re the one who ended things. Preparing for pain somewhat inures you against it. If you’re attending weddings around the time you were meant to be married, it’s quite likely that you’ll be the topic of conversation or even subjected to outright intrusiveness. If you can’t handle the side-eyes or gossip, don’t attend. If you do attend, don’t make a spectacle of yourself. Whatever you do, don’t be a drunken slob. There’s no moral or egotistical victory to be won by attending. I’d even recommend the high road and, if possible, let them know you won’t be there so they’re not walking on eggshells. Not everyone needs to know you did the leaving and why. If your ex feels the need to save face by making you the jilted instead of the jiltee, allow them this small grace. There might be occasions when your friends will feel like they need to defend your honour out of loyalty. Tell them exactly what and how much is okay to share, so they’re spared the mental gymnastics. If you’re the friend who has to establish that your bestie isn’t, in fact, an irredeemable villain, stick to the approved script no matter how much you’re itching to set the record straight. …but it’s not okay to be guillotined for acting in your best interests. A polite-but-firm “moving on” to change topics is perfectly acceptable when Detective Do-Gooder decides to make your business their business. Travel. Sit this wedding season out, regardless of whose wedding you’re missing. If your wedding’s been called off because you cheated, there’s no way the sordid details haven’t made the rounds. …and that none of it will be kind to you, a lot of it will reach you. When that happens, keep your crashouts (there will be many) private. When the invariable “But what the hell happened?” question rolls around, don’t lie, don’t try to justify, don’t try to play the victim. Even if you think you had reasons for cheating, keep them to yourself. “I made a mistake” is a perfectly adequate comment. Even if you’re in a relationship with them now, the wedding season is not the time to go official. Seeming too gleeful will make you come off as petty and crass. Do the decent thing and pretend to feel bad. Bitterness is aggressively unappealing at weddings, even for a bride-that-wasn’t. It might be economical, but it’s also pathetic and cartoonish. If you can’t be civil in public, don’t attend weddings together. Be very careful about what you say. Families have a way of magically resolving issues overnight (or, better still, pretending they never existed at all). They might forgive each other, but they won’t forgive you. It’s just going to make you sound pitiful and prolong the cycle of misery. “We’ll let you know when we have a date” is sufficient engagement with self-appointed town criers. Don’t run around declaring the time of death on the couple. You don’t want to be the friend who had no faith if the wedding actually gets resuscitated.

In the end, Ashima and Garv’s wedding wasn’t designed to dazzle. It was simply a reflection of who they are. Thoughtful. Warm. A little nostalgic. A little modern. And quietly certain of where they’re headed together.

article_title: Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding had approximately 10 lakh flowers
sub_title: We speak to Interflora India’s founder, Anuja Joshi, who played a pivotal role in beautifying Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding in Udaipur
article_content: There are weddings that trend and there are weddings that become the talk of the town. Then there are weddings where every little detail is so extravagant, so excessive, that the entire internet wants to get involved. The recent nuptials of billionaire heiress But how many flowers does it actually take to break the internet? 10 lakh flower stems and 800 florists is the floral math behind Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding. “Three rounds of floral sampling were done with the bride alone. Netra knew exactly what she wanted. The florals had to honour the sanctity of Indian culture yet be styled in a distinctly European manner,” says Anuja Joshi, founder at Interflora India. “No chrysanthemums, no carnations, no daisies and none of the typical “filler flowers” made the cut. Ranunculus featured at every event as Netra loves them.” Each colour and flower served a purpose; nothing was used just to fill space. “Inspired by ‘navratna’ (the nine cosmic jewels believed to harmonise and bless new beginnings), the wedding unfolded across six events in different palatial settings where we assigned every event its own hero flower which spoke to the bride’s taste,” Joshi added. Burgundy hydrangeas accordingly led the way to the Welcome Dinner, while the peach-and-orange fruit-inspired palette for the haldi was set against a bougainvillaea canopy. The Cirque du Soleil–inspired mehendi was a nod to one of the couple’s early dates, with deep purple alliums turning the celebration into a mini dreamscape. A Bollywood-meets-opera sangeet drifted into pink monochrome with phalaenopsis and peonies as showstoppers. The wedding ceremony bloomed with white hydrangeas while the reception closed the festivities with a pristine cloud of white phalaenopsis. For a wedding of this scale, floral emergencies are practically accounted for, except the one at Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding looked like it had stepped out of the pages of a fairytale. “All the wedding flowers that were meant to arrive three days before the wedding only landed the evening before. Picture this: thousands of fresh-cut blooms landed at the venue at 5pm, and because this was Jagmandir Island Palace, the only way to bring them in was by water. Cue boatloads and midnight sprints to pull off the early morning wedding setup in record time,” Joshi recalls. The wedding came with its own logistical ballet of flipping multiple heritage venues in impossible timelines, backstage transitions on clockwork and a 15,000sqft cold room built solely to store the flowers. While people assume viral weddings are only about the grand pieces and monumental installations, Netra Mantena and Vamsi Gadiraju’s wedding achieved a sweet balance. “Grandeur isn’t in piling more things but in detailing and layering. Udaipur is not your average venue—it’s a living museum of centuries-old domes and palatial walls, so the decor should never compete with but complement the architecture,” Joshi explains. The Interflora team decked the palace walls with never-before-seen green cascades and purple delphiniums to elevate the guest walkway at City Palace’s Manek Chowk for the mehendi function. Later, for the nuptials at the Jagmandir Island Palace, the existing central dome was reimagined as the mandap, resembling a temple in the middle of a lake adorned with traditional South Indian flowers. The backdrop featured a floral-crafted Shri Yantra (a geometric symbol comprising nine interlocking triangles that are considered powerful in Hindu and Buddhist traditions), transforming the space into a site of spiritual resonance. In a land of extravagant weddings, it takes something exceptionally unique to make an Indian wedding go viral, but Joshi says the Interflora team doesn’t operate from a place of chasing likes and comments. “You never design a wedding with the intention of making it go viral; instead, you design knowing it will withstand the emotional weight of the day. It’s never about turning every corner into a photo-op but finding those two or three special spots that naturally become everyone’s favourite backdrop; the places that spark joy and end up living in family albums long after the wedding is over,” she smiles.

article_title: Bridal skincare that works with your hormones, not against them
sub_title: Experts explain how hormones, sleep and nutrition shape your skincare results more than last-minute facials ever could
article_content: The weeks leading up to the wedding can feel like an emotional seesaw: excitement giving way to anxiety, joy interrupted by late-night planning spirals and a constant chorus of advice on what to do (and absolutely not do) as a part of your bridal skincare routine. Slather this, massage that—your skincare arsenal does its thing, but real radiance depends on your gut and hormones running in sync. If skin could ask for one thing in the days leading up to the wedding, Dr Sravya Tipirneni, consultant dermatologist, cosmetologist and trichologist at Manipal Hospitals, Bengaluru, says it would be a simple plea: “Slow down. I need water, sleep and zero new products. Treat me gently; I’m not a dress you can tailor last minute.” "Your skin is essentially a hormone-responsive organ,” says Dr Asha Dalal, director of obstetrics and gynaecology at Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, Mumbai. “Hormones influence almost every layer, from oil production and hydration to According to Dr Dalal, the sweet spot for what people call the “bridal glow” is the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, roughly days six to fourteen. “Oestrogen rises steadily during this period,” she says. “It boosts collagen formation, increases The luteal phase—the seven to ten days before your period—is the moodier half. “Skin is more reactive, oilier and more likely to break out,” she warns, which makes last-minute experimentation risky. Dr Dalal’s rule is straightforward: laser treatments, microneedling and chemical peels should be done four to eight weeks before the wedding, ideally aligned with the follicular phase, when healing is quicker. In her words, a menstrual cycle becomes a beauty calendar when you understand how it behaves. The smallest missteps can snowball. “A night of poor sleep can dull the skin, but a few in a row can spike cortisol enough to slow collagen repair,” says Dr Tipirneni. We often underestimate how fatigue shows up on the face. Over-scheduling only compounds it. “Schedule daily tech-free mental downtime (15–30 minutes) and prioritise 7–9 hours of sleep.” Just as important is restraint. “Implement a strict hands-off rule. It’s the easiest way to keep a tiny blemish from becoming a lasting scar.” Food decides whether the glow holds or falters. Functional medicine nutritionist and lifestyle educator Karishmma Chawla puts it bluntly: “Gluten, dairy, processed foods, sugar, packaged foods with hidden gluten or industrial starch, they don’t vibe with your skin story.” They stoke “Hormones adore high-quality protein,” she says. “When your diet balances proteins and fats well, that’s what shapes your hormone language.” Acne flare-ups, in her framework, are simply messages from the body: a nudge to pay attention. Her “bridal glow grocery list” is a pared-back, functional ritual. Pick up one low-GI fruit (apple, pear, guava, berries or orange), one green ( Cold-pressed coconut oil, herbs and pepper form “a magical concoction” that supports thyroid function, keeps harmful bacteria in check and lends skin a plush finish. Fermented foods—kefir, kombucha, pickled vegetables—enter the picture only when the gut is on steadier ground. Caffeine, meanwhile, is the subtle saboteur. “You don’t have to quit coffee; just stop letting it open the show,” she says. Start the day with lukewarm water and lime or aloe, or go straight to your smoothie, and save your lightest brew for later. Everything eventually finds its way back to cortisol. “Anything that doesn’t align with your gut spikes cortisol because your body thinks danger is near,” Chawla explains. High cortisol steals progesterone—the hormone that soothes—slows thyroid function, alters metabolism and invites bloating, acidity and dullness. “Foods that love you back make your body feel safe.” When the gut is calm, the hormones are steady and the mind is rested, the skin mirrors that peace. The makeup, the facials, the dress–they’re the finishing bows. The radiance underneath is self-built. And as Chawla says, “The outer glow is really just a reflection of the inner healing: food, lifestyle and purpose.”

article_title: Your go-to skincare guide for the ultimate pre-wedding glow up
sub_title: If you’re a bride-to-be, here’s the secret to achieving brighter, smoother-looking skin from within for that unmistakable wedding-day glow
article_content: Every bride dreams of that unmistakable wedding-day glow, the kind that makes you look effortlessly radiant on your big day. But between nonstop planning, late nights, and the constant whirlwind of emotions, that glow can easily get lost somewhere between your to-do lists and the demands on your time. The days leading up to a wedding are anything but calm. Schedules are packed, sleep becomes optional, and hydration is something we remember only when our skin starts feeling flaky. Between fittings, family gatherings, and travel, your skin barely gets a moment to recover. Add pollution, stress, erratic sleep, and less-than-ideal eating habits, and it’s no surprise your complexion begins to show fatigue, dullness, and uneven texture. But skincare shouldn’t just sit on the surface—it should work Think of your glow as something that’s built over time. Sure, the facials and organic masks will help, but they can only do so much. Quick fixes may give instant results, but they often don’t last. article_title: How to keep your skin sane through a marathon of destination weddings
sub_title: For wedding guests racing through flights, feasts and shifting climates, with expert advice to keep your skin steady through it all
article_content: On a recent trip to Jaipur for a family wedding, my skin was crying for mercy. Decadent Rajasthani feasts, makeup going on and coming off every few hours, three nights of four-hour sleep and a sudden climate switch turned my face into a cautionary tale. That’s when it struck me that the pursuit of the wedding glow isn’t just the bride’s anymore. Because the modern wedding calendar looks more like a travel itinerary. From Jaisalmer to Jaipur and Phuket to Portofino, your skin is expected to keep up as you hop from one flight to another for more than one happy couple this season. The beauty brief now includes the jet-setting guest, sprinting through ceremonies, red-eye flights and humidity swings, fuelled by equal parts SPF and sheer willpower. As India’s destination weddings evolve into multi-day marathons across climates and time zones, your skincare routine needs to be as versatile and resilient as Athletes train their bodies to run long distances, lift weights to sustain muscle recovery, hydrate well before the big day and get ample rest. Multi-day wedding functions require resilience too. Jet lag shows up on my face. By the time you get off a flight, whatever radiance you have built during the pre-wedding routine has evaporated somewhere over the Arabian Sea. Cabin air steals moisture, circulation slows and that lit-from-within glow fades fast. Add hard hotel water to the mix and the The antidote is a post-flight reset built on deep hydration, soft cleansing and barrier-loving formulas that coax the complexion back to life just in time for the celebrations. Dr Agarwal's go-to ritual: hydrate well, avoid alcohol in flight, cleanse with a rich Different climates rewrite the skin’s entire rulebook. If desert-like heat thins skin barrier, then a shift to a humid weather like Udaipur or Mumbai unfolds the opposite chaos–sweat, sebum and microbes creating a lush playground for congestion and fungal flare-ups. Going up North to places like Delhi and Chandigarh pollution rises, PM levels spike and the skin’s defences work overtime, leaving it inflamed, sensitised and prone to I put a long-standing packing dilemma to the skin experts: if we had room for just five skincare essentials during a destination wedding week, what should make the cut? Here’s what they recommended. Weddings rarely allow for a full routine, but dermatologists agree on the one thing you can’t skip: sunscreen. “Dehydration and breakouts can be fixed, sun damage can’t,” says Dr Agarwal. Another common oversight is failing to adapt products to the climate, and cleansing properly becomes essential. “Makeup wipes aren’t enough. You need water and a real cleanser.” Dr Sethi adds that a stealth culprit behind wedding-fatigue breakouts is the communal brush kit passed around in glam rooms. As indulgent as having on-call makeup artists feel, shared tools are a fast track to acne. My workaround is simple enough. I hand the artist my own brushes, the creativity stays and the breakouts don’t. Ultimately, wedding-season beauty is a test of stamina. The glow chase is no longer the bride's alone, so I’m already getting ready for my next round of destination weddings. If this is an endurance sport, I plan to finish strong.

article_title: How to put together a work outfit that you actually like

article_content: If you’ve ever found yourself at the receiving end of a “This is a school, not a fashion show” reprimand because your skirt was hitched an inch too high, entering the corporate world as an adult can dredge up some embarrassing memories. Unless, of course, you were to make the office your runway. The average officegoer spends a significant amount of their life under fluorescent lights, shuffling between meetings and coffee runs, before slowly dissolving into monotony. So if the corporate world insists on consuming most of your waking hours, the least it can do is bear witness to a fabulous fit. It’s time to shake up those tired corporate dress codes and take a leaf out of the books of these three professionals. “I’m in the office four to five times a week from 9 to 5, that’s a considerable amount of my life,” shares Awan. “If I look my best, I feel good. I work in an environment where I never know who I’m going to meet. And every encounter is an opportunity for a great first impression.” Awan gravitates towards tailoring—suits, Accessories are where Awan has fun, “I love Awan's work outfit staples include: Finance isn’t known for encouraging fashion risks, but Kat has carved out a style that feels both personal and unfussy. Her philosophy is simple: start where you are. “It doesn’t have to be zero to a hundred,” she says. “You can introduce pieces gradually and see how they make you feel and how they’re received.” Those small choices build confidence. “If it feels right, keep going,” she says. “Even something small like a sculptural For Kat, practicality is important: “If you’re already running late and you’ve got to pull an ironing board out, it’s game over,” she says. Comfort, however, can be negotiated. “I often sacrifice comfort if it means the outfit comes together beautifully. I commute in heels more often than I should, but at the same time, comfort and style don’t have to be mutually exclusive.” Her wardrobe reflects that reality: wide-leg trousers, crisp shirts and Kat is also firmly anti-trend. “One of my greatest fears is walking into a room wearing the same thing as someone else,” she says. “I’d have no choice but to go home.” That approach has helped her build a wardrobe she actually enjoys. “It makes getting dressed exciting,” she says. “It feels like I’m constantly inventing and reinventing.” Crucially, her clothes haven’t undermined her credibility. “Once people see that your professionalism and output are unaffected by how you dress, those preconceptions fade away.” Kat's work outfit staples include: Lyndem’s approach to office dressing is uncomplicated. “The day I want to wear neutrals, I’ll wear neutrals,” she says. “The day I want to be colourful, I’ll wear colourful clothes.” Her style is eclectic, intuitive and driven by mood rather than rules. “Sometimes the colour combinations I choose are something I’ve just seen on the street, like the wall outside a shop and its shutters. Colour is everywhere in India, so it’s quite easy.” Experimentation is key. “You’re just going to have to mix and match and try everything,” she says. “You try everything and make do with whatever you have. If I see something trendy or something I like, I’ll get it stitched,” she explains, which allows her to personalise trends rather than replicate them. That same mindset carries into traditional wear. article_title: Samantha Ruth Prabhu’s pistachio Banarasi silk sari is hand-beaten patua zari
sub_title: The actor paired her Label Sourav Das drape with emerald jewellery
article_content: On Republic Day, Samantha Ruth Prabhu made her way to the Rashtrapati Bhavan for the At Home reception after receiving an invite from President Droupadi Murmu. For the occasion, the south star wore heritage on her sleeves, turning to a revival Banarasi Iktara weave from the Label Sourav Das. Rendered in a pistachio green that looks time-honoured yet freshly calibrated for now, the sari breaks from the primary jewel tones typically associated with Banarasi drapes. The silk canvas is scattered with gold woven buttis, while a rich border and pallu elevates it. “Samantha’s is wearing a quintessential Hazar Buiti Asharfi Sikka revival Banarasi sari with a bygone angri border woven in finer counts of mulberry silk. It also has konias on either side of the pallu. The sari is woven with Kaduwa method in Iktara style with hand-beaten patua zari,” shares Sourav Das. The Iktara, also known as single thread, technique offers not just strength and smoothness but also a fluid fall and a resilient life that’s prized by connoisseurs. Banarasi saris have long occupied a rarefied place in Indian wardrobes. Their lineage traces back centuries of royal patronage and painstaking craftsmanship. One weave can take weeks, sometimes months, to complete, with master weavers translating complex designs onto looms that demand memory and muscle. What makes them singular is not just the silk or the zari, but the varied motifs, from florals nodding to abundance, to paisley border, signifying fertility and eternity. In the actor’s sari, the geometric buttis, which speaks of cosmic order, feels particularly resonant. It serves an emblem of continuity for a woman who has repeatedly chosen longevity over trend. She completed the look with an open-setting diamond and emerald choker, complemented by matching stud earrings and a statement ring from Golecha’s Jewels. Her hair was worn in a sleek, middle-parted half-up, half-down style, while her makeup stayed understated and refined with a matte, skin-like base, softly smoked eyes and a nude lip that let the jewellery and weave take the spotlight. A pistachio sari and jewels, like hers, is a smart trousseau investment. While it is timeless in spirit, it is refreshingly modern and versatile enough to move seamlessly from intimate family ceremonies to landmark events for years to come.

article_title: A life beautifully lived—Hamish Bowles remembers Valentino
sub_title: Valentino Garavani conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a certain idea of beauty to all he touched
article_content: Valentino Clemente Ludovico Garavani—known, simply and powerfully, as Valentino—was born on May 11th, 1932, in Voghera, a rather quiet place lost somewhere between Milan and Genoa. But by the time he died, aged 93, on January 19, he had conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a “I love beauty—it’s not my fault,” Valentino famously said with a shrug, and in fashion, he saw a way to captivate and ensnare women (his only clients when starting out, before he widened the purview of his well-dressed net). He trained at the Accademia dell’Arte in Milan, studying both French and fashion, and then, aged 17, moved to Paris, to the École des Beaux-Arts and the Chambre Syndicale de la Couture, before securing an apprenticeship in 1951 with the Athenian couturier Jean Dessès, who dressed royalty and high society ladies in his immaculately draped and vividly colored evening gowns. Jacqueline, the Comtesse de Ribes, dressed with Dessès, and when she was asked by Oleg Cassini to design some dresses for him in Paris, she mentioned it to Dessès, telling the designer that “I don’t know how to draw in a chic way.” Dessès was amused. “I have an Italian illustrator,” he told her, “who would be very happy to earn a little more money after working-hours doing the drawings for you”, and a friendship between Valentino and Jacqueline was born. When he was When Guy Laroche, Dessès’s assistant, departed to start his own couture house, Valentino joined him for a few years before leaving to work briefly with the Russian-Georgian Princess Irene Galitzine (Galitzine had made palazzo pyjamas a thing, amidst opulent evening clothes). Then, in 1959, Valentino started his own house with backing from his father and a family friend. In the meantime, someone had come into his life. Giancarlo Giammetti recently recalled their first meeting, with Giammetti seated alone in a Roman cafe. “A kind person came and said, ‘Are you alone?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ ‘Do you mind if me and my friend can sit here?’ Of course,” Giammetti remembered. “And Valentino sat next to me—I remember very deeply.” A whoosh of dark hair framed Valentino’s tanned face, with its sultry features and his arresting blue eyes. “Then Valentino started to speak to me in French. I said, ‘Sorry?’ ‘Oh, sorry—I just arrived from Paris after seven years, my mind goes French, and I was hoping that you speak French…’” Giammetti, it turns out, had studied French for most of his life. “He said, ‘From now on, if I see you again, we speak French.’ And we still do. Incredibly.” The two would speak French to each other—as lovers, and then as intimate friends and business partners—for the rest of Valentino’s life. Valentino soon found a lavish, frescoed apartment in the fashionable Via Condotti, but less than a year later, he was facing bankruptcy. (Though Valentino threw the blame at his “champagne tastes,” someone had not been paying the rent.) He and Giammetti simply moved the salon to a 16th-century palazzo on the Via Gregoriana. (Incidentally, Giammetti acquired the Via Condotti apartment recently and has had it transformed into his offices by Studio Peregalli’s Laura Sartori Rimini. It’s a sumptuous series of rooms, the walls now hung with silver tissue or silk velvet—though some still have their original frescoes—and filled with Hervé van der Straten furniture and antiques. What may have been “Champagne tastes” in 1959 are now sublime and defining.) Valentino gradually began to make his mark on fashion. His flashing good looks easily summoned the press, to be sure, but it was his clothes that had an allure for the stars who would pass through Rome. And when Elizabeth Taylor, there to shoot Suddenly, his work was appearing in As Valentino became a name to watch, with ladies—Audrey Hepburn, Sophia Loren, any number of princesses, Jaqueline Kennedy Onassis, Nan Kempner, Lynn Wyatt, and Susan Gutfreund, among so many more, flocking to dress with him—so his residences became exponentially more impressive. His Roman base—a penthouse apartment with Persian miniatures on the fabric-covered walls and banquettes fit for a Turkish salon, had been transformed into a house on the Appian Way, decorated by Renzo Mongiardino, the When I first went to Rome for the couture in the mid-’80s, long before my Appian Way adventure, I plucked up all my courage and walked into Valentino’s intimidating couture salon just off the top of the Spanish steps—two small-ish rooms that positively oozed with Of course, this pair of elegantly finished rooms opened onto a positive hive of industry occupying five floors of a vast palazzo. Here were the couture ateliers: room after room of industrious ladies and a smattering of men—hundreds of them—applied to the task at hand in light-flooded rooms. (Some years after my first adventure with the couture salon, the place was subtly transformed by the English architects and designers Peter Moore and Peter Kent—there were silvered bannisters, acres of pale grey marble in the hallways, and paintings by Julian Schnabel, Keith Haring, and Francesco Clemente, and it was all very, very chic.) Valentino’s show then always finished with music just before the In 1991, I had an appointment with Valentino to discuss his entire career, and met with him in an elegant room looking over the Piazza Mignanelli, filled with antiques and lush draperies that lent it a Cécile Sorel sort of look. It was not easy getting him to speak. Next door in a vast room—and I mean Of course, Valentino had a number of other properties: in Capri, in New York, in London. But in 1995, I was invited to the 17th century chateau of brick and stone he had acquired—a house that was revealed to me only after I had followed a drive and dramatically turned a corner: There, plunging downhill, and glimmering below, was the Chateau de Wideville, once home to Madame de la Valliere, mistress of Louis XIV (Versailles is conveniently near). In the evening’s light, I explored the breathtaking Jacques Wirtz gardens, where brilliant violet rosemary stretched across the field and cut through the forests, while roses and scented high-summer flowers filled the walled garden. And then: the breathtaking house itself. Valentino worked with Henri Samuel on the interiors, which—with their emerald silk-velvet armchairs and a sort of Chinoiserie motif, which gave the house a sort of fanciful Palm Beach air—brought a level of comfort to the splendidly austere exterior. I was amused to see that the enormous Francis Bacon in Valentino’s sitting room depicted an abstracted man sitting on a carpet of bunches of roses, quite unlike anything I had seen before in his work—as Valentino-ish as it was possible for a Bacon to be. As I headed in for dinner, rather moved by the exquisite gardens and the ravishing interiors—by everything that Giancarlo and Valentino had done in life—I said to Valentino, “What you’ve done is to create beauty.” He clasped my hand and, weeping, said, “It

article_title: Shanaya Kapoor’s Anita Dongre lehenga is brought to life with hand-painted Pichhwai
sub_title: Hand-painted flora and fauna move across the surface, layered with antique work that gives the piece a tactile richness
article_content: When it comes to occasionwear, Shanaya Kapoor consistently returns to pieces designed to last. Her latest pick, an Featuring a strappy blouse and a billowing skirt, the ensemble’s silk base lends a diaphanousness that mirrors Kapoor’s pared-back approach to ceremonial dressing. Set against a distinctive meadow greenish-yellow, the lehenga immediately stands apart for its nature-inspired hue. Motifs take centre stage in the look, in sync with Dongre's signature design language. The hand-painted Pichhwai artwork unfolds across the lehenga like a living landscape, populated with blooming florals, foliage, wildlife and fluttering birds. The blouse reflects the same story and is further elevated with intricate surface techniques. A delicate organza dupatta brings the ensemble together, offering a gentler counterpoint to the richly detailed lehenga. The ensemble draws its soul from the art of Pichhwai painting, a 400-year-old craft that originated in Rajasthan in the 16th century. Traditionally created as devotional backdrops depicting tales of Shrinathji, Pichhwai paintings were also deeply inspired by the rhythms of nature, from seasons to flora and fauna. In the lehenga, this heritage is reinterpreted with each motif meticulously hand-painted by skilled artisans and delicately enhanced with sequins. The lehenga took close to 90 days to create, a timeline that honours the patience and attention this craft demands. The piece is animated by an in-house master painter, whose deep-rooted Pichhwai lineage informs every brushstroke. As the designer shared, this lehenga is part of the House of Anita Dongre’s larger effort to ensure that art forms like Pichhwai continue to thrive within a contemporary language. She accessorised with intricate temple jewellery from Indinoor. A gold necklace adorned with bird motifs carried on the lehenga’s avian motifs, paired with statement jhumkas and kaan chains that were attached to her loose braid. For her beauty look, she stuck with dewy makeup in warm copper tones for a soft, sun-kissed finish.

Given the strength of the blouse, stylist Tanya Ghavri took a measured step back when it came to accessorising the look with jewellery. Thanks to the high neckline, she gave a necklace a rain check. Soft glam defined the makeup, with a dewy base, gentle smoky eyes and glossy pink lips to keep things fresh. The sleek updo, too, felt inspired by yesteryears, completing the nostalgia-led narrative. What makes a look, like Sutaria’s sari, enduring is its versatility. The ivory palette acts as a blank canvas, allowing it to shift seamlessly across seasons and occasions. For daytime pheras, it feels serene and ceremonial, while a switch to a bold red pout, gemstone jewellery or sharper eye makeup can instantly take it into cocktail territory.

article_title: The digital Vintage Casio watch is bending time in 2025
sub_title: From a certain NYC mayor to your style influencer cousin, simple 20th-century timepieces like Casio’s A1000MA series have become everyone’s go-to accessories.
article_content: As I stand on an uneven platform for the next train, I am presented with my current favourite fashion show—the New York subway. You can spot a fall/winter ’25 And this isn’t just a New York thing. Over the last two months, I’ve started noticing the same glint everywhere I go. In Tokyo, it’s the clear-resin variants; in Seoul, the retro golds; in Mumbai cafés, the classic F91W that refuses to retire. One September afternoon in Bandra, outside a tiny post-production studio, a filmmaking student waited for his auto wearing a block-printed kurta and a gold-toned Casio LA670. A week later in Delhi, during a quick coffee run in Meherchand Market, a If you glance around, you’ll also spot the odd Seiko Rotocall and Q Timex, but somehow, it is vintage Casio watches that are dominating the conversation. Especially, the A1000MA-7—and somehow the entire Casio Vintage family has found itself back in the cultural spotlight. History was first made with the release of the Casiotron (QW02-10) in 1974—the world’s first fully digital wristwatch with an automatic calendar—but it was never just a timekeeper. Over the years, Casio digital watches have become pop-culture fixtures, appearing everywhere from on-screen sci-fi fantasies including They remain a staple of This lineage, from the pioneering Casiotron to the cult-classic F-91W of the 1990s, leads directly to today’s A1000 models. They carry the same retro credibility and matte-metal minimalism, now elevated with polished stainless steel and a Milanese strap. It’s this blend of historic tech cool and modern refinement that makes wearing the watch both disarmingly ordinary and unexpectedly iconic. “It’s one of the few timepieces that slips into anyone’s life without demanding a costume change,” says stylist Ayesha Amin Nigam, who has been spotting them on shoots across Delhi and Mumbai. She tells me that, in the last year alone, she’s seen them on interns, models, production assistants, even accountants who wander on set in between takes. “It shapeshifts into whatever the outfit needs—grounding streetwear, sharpening suiting or sitting quietly against a The variants alone could fill a moodboard: the brushed-steel A1000MA, its gold-toned MG counterpart, the pastel-tinted MPR editions, the ultra-slim LA670s, and even the resin-cased F-series that collectors love for its purist ’80s silhouette. And unlike many vintage icons, most of these models are still in production and available directly at brand stores, while a handful of discontinued colourways and older A1000 batches quietly trade hands on resale platforms like My Almari and Luxepolis for those seeking a deeper There is another reality that also exists: Christie’s Geneva Luxury Week reported sales of 21,641,435 Swiss francs (approximately ₹242 crores) in rare watches, with a significant 34% of the bidders being millennials and Gen Z’ers. If younger consumers are willing to spend big at auction, why are modest, sub-₹20,000 digital Casios suddenly the cultural touchstone? Part of the answer lies in accessibility, nostalgia and the social currency of effortless style. “Casio democratised digital timekeeping long before it was fashionable,” explains Sarosh Mody, founder of Luxury Watch Works, an after-sales boutique based in Mumbai. “The G-Shock, for example, became—and remains—a cultural icon. Its popularity reflects the people’s choice, not marketing, not snob value. Casio understood utility decades before smartwatches were conceived. The calculator, TV, radio and camera watches were made by them way before the Swiss even thought about them. The brand has blurred the line between Today, reissues and collaborations like the Timex T80 x Maison Margiela and Omega x Swatch drops show that design credibility doesn’t need a luxury price tag. Together, these watches have become a global shorthand for personality, nostalgia and style that crosses generations and geographies. And style icons and collectors continue the trend: Casio watches were a mainstay of But why this watch and why now? I suspect that it’s because it is fundamentally reminiscent of a simpler time. The only complication in the watch is an alarm, just like the one you would wear in school, beeping at the end of an exam. It’s something you perhaps spotted on your father back in the day, and till today, it rings a bell. A personal connection in your wardrobe that tells a story: perhaps that’s the ultimate style flex.

article_title: Tara Sutaria’s floral skirt set is a comfortable alternative to heavy lehengas

article_content: For her intimate Christmas celebrations at home, Tara Sutaria chose a look that straddled intimacy with high drama. Though technically a modern co-ord set, Sutaria’s look by Gauri & Nainika reads as something far more versatile. Inching towards a compelling alternative to an ornate lehenga, it appears equally suited to a destination wedding soirée where modernity is prized as much as tradition. At first glance, the ensemble feels like a modern-day lehenga reimagined through a contemporary lens. Comprising a high-waisted, billowing, floor-grazing skirt and a sculpted bralette, the set is lifted by painterly florals that bloom against a noir base. The ensemble is drawn from Gauri & Nainika’s Lakmē Fashion Week x FDCI Spring–Summer 2026 showcase, where the designer duo unveiled a collection rooted in wearable artistry. Inspired by painted canvases, dark roses and moody still lifes, the line translated romance into tactile form using organza, tulle and silk mikado, shaping silhouettes defined by volume, bows, ruffles and drama. On Sutaria, these themes distilled into a maximalist floral piece that felt opulent and of-the-moment. Black punctuated with bold florals has long held fashion’s imagination, from the late '30s’ bias-cut evening gowns to the lacquered rose prints of the ‘50s. This lineage is mirrored on her look. The high-waisted skirt elongates the frame, offering a sleek, cinched foundation, while the bralette’s open back introduces a sensual counterpoint. A sleek, centre-parted bun was adorned with red roses, complemented by a deep crimson lip, together conjuring a Frida Kahlo-esque romanticism. article_title: 2025 is the year we pledged allegiance to the tabi shoe
sub_title: The horse hoof-lookalikes are no longer just on the runway—they are also next to you on the Mumbai local.
article_content: In an era of touch-and-go trends, no one would have imagined that shoes that look like horse hooves would have staying power. Back in 2023, when The controversial shoe has always been highly endorsed. In 1988, Let’s just say if you made a drinking game out of every time you saw a certified cool person in tabis, it would not end well for your nervous system. And the bug spreads well beyond celebrities. From the streets of Central Saint Martins in London to the Mumbai local, from Dua Lipa to Naina Bhan to “We’re the first generation with instant access to global fashion. Our appetite to experiment has never been stronger,” says Akanksha Rathore, the founder of lifestyle brand Kilchu. “We saw this as an interesting opportunity to define tabis in the context of Indian juttis.” At Kilchu, you can pick between hand-painted leather styles in aquamarine, salmon or a dark brown that quite literally passes as a horse hoof. That’s not all: even athleisure brands like Nike and Reebok have explored sneakerina split toes. And you know the hype is real when a trend transcends the chronically online and makes it to the glitzy shaadi circuit, as is the case with the golden tabi heels from Chal Jooti. Before you roll your eyes at the dupe-fication of Margiela, it’s essential to note that the tabis were not invented by the French. Their provenance can be traced back to 15th-century Japan, where these were worn as socks, separating the big toe from the rest to maintain grip, balance and comfort. By the early 20th century, rubber soles strengthened the slip ons, creating the style we now call tabis. In fact, the so-called luxury design is still commonly worn by labourers in Japan. Could it be that the internet’s obsession with Hobonichi planners, Studio Ghibli, matcha and all things East Asia summoned the return of the tabis? Well perhaps. But if you ask stylist and designer Jayati Monga, an ardent wearer of the In truth, the central conflict of the tabi—the ‘will they, won’t they’—is a major draw for many wearers. At a time when everything from your inside-joke laptop sticker to the DIY crochet keychain on your bag is a way to script your personality, wearing tabis signals which niche you bend the knee for. It is a strange IYKYK declaration, attracting those who subscribe to similar experimentation while weeding out others who are scared to err on the wrong side of fashion. In fact Monga influenced her flatmate to join the tabi tribe. “They felt super out there to me at first but I love how whimsical tabis can look,” says Udisha Madan, 27, who has just ordered her split-toe shoes. Most people will agree, the hoof lookalikes do not evoke love at first sight. Just like other great works of art—Lena Dunham’s Another factor, I suspect, that makes the design covetable is how gatekept it continues to be. In all honesty, even at its peak, the split-toe style will never become as popular as Docs, Birks or Crocs. However, that is also the point. The moment the controversial shoe wholly sinks into the mainstream, it will lose its appeal or intrigue. No one is going to ask you why you’re wearing horse hooves if everyone is wearing horse hooves.

article_title: Archival fashion was everywhere in 2025
sub_title: Archival fashion became one of the most visible styling choices, shaped by nostalgia and an increasingly crowded trend landscape
article_content: Fashion has always loved a comeback story, but lately, it has become more of a headline-maker. Archival fashion looks get social media traction, headlines and conversation, whether it’s a decades-old gown resurfacing on a red carpet or a vintage silhouette reworked through a contemporary lens. This return to the past reads as aesthetic, emotional and commercial. The current cultural instability, coupled with economic jitters and the exhaustion of the hyper-digital world that we live in has amplified the effect of the nostalgic cycle on fashion. When the present doesn’t meet our emotional needs, we look back, often with rose-tinted glasses. Every era had its own distinct fashion zeitgeist, from Y2K maximalism to the ‘90s grunge and hip-hop, and the preppy style of the ‘80s. Today’s landscape, by contrast, feels fragmented with the chaos of microtrends and overconsumption. In a market flooded with duplicates and lookalikes, vintage fashion reads as more authentic, proof of taste, effort and discernment. It offers a way to stand apart from an algorithm built on sameness. “Fashion wasn’t safe, and collections weren’t designed primarily around sales projections. That freedom produced work that still resonates today in a way that much of today’s more cautious fashion doesn’t,” says Allia Al Rufai, fashion stylist and consultant. Fashion has the capacity to shape culture in ways that extend far beyond the runway. Certain garments have become cultural markers, referenced and remembered decades later because they captured a moment with emotional force. That kind of resonance takes time, experimentation and, often, the willingness to fail. Today, the balance between artistry and business is often off-kilter. Creativity is expected to move at the speed of commerce, leaving little room for evolution. “Fashion cycles are much faster, critiques are immediate, and new creatives at heritage houses aren’t allowed enough time to experiment. They’re constantly compared to their predecessors, even before their vision has fully formed,” says SJ Singh, a fashion and culture analyst. Although designers across the world continue to push boundaries, the broader mood has changed. Iconicity rarely happens overnight. For something to become iconic, there has to be room for error and growth, a window that for some has narrowed significantly under the pressure of social media. When celebrities step out in carefully chosen pieces from a designer’s past, the response is immediate. These looks arrive with a built-in narrative, a recognisable image and a sense of intentionality that cuts through the noise. Archival dressing becomes cultural shorthand, signalling discernment rather than trend-chasing. It’s also why these moments travel so effectively. They encourage research and recognition, making it a conversation rather than a disposable moment. The resurgence of archival fashion today can feel like a retreat but perhaps is also a response to a present shaped by metrics and viral marketing. Fashion was never meant to exist solely for algorithms or rapid consumption. At its most powerful, it has been culturally tied, emotionally resonant and allowed the time to breathe. If archival fashion feels newly compelling now, it may be because it carries traces of that slower rhythm, one we are still learning how to recover.

article_title: Karisma Kapoor’s beige Ritu Kumar anarkali relies on the power of construction
sub_title: Intricate threadwork elevates her suit set
article_content: For a recent outing, Karisma Kapoor opted for a beige kurta set from Ritu Kumar, which at a cursory glance seems pared-down but on a closer look, it’s intricate and commanding. The look’s neutral palette serves as a reminder that impact does not always rely on colour saturation. The silhouette is classic anarkali, but it is reimagined with a slightly jacket-style construction. Ritu Kumar’s beige Begum suit set unfolds with a thoughtful balance of heritage and ease. Crafted in Chanderi silk, the anarkali is structured at the bodice, where fine embroidery traces the form flowing into the fluid, flared skirt. The silhouette moves with grace, while a complementary tulle dupatta adds a diaphanous layer of lightness. Together, the elements create a look that feels ceremonial yet wearable. The embroidery deserves a special mention. Executed in resham threads, its colours draw from autumnal hues, including muted ambers, soft olives and burnished golds, and are shaped into delicate florals and foliage. A scooped back introduces a subtle sensuality and a counterpoint to the otherwise modest ensemble. Central to the outfit’s appeal is its fabric. Chanderi, often described by local artisans as “booni hui hawa” or woven air, is prized for its breathability and feather-light feel. Its ability to remain airy through humidity and transitional weather makes it ideal for Indian festivities that stretch across monsoon, autumn and winter. Long celebrated for its delicate transparency and understated lustre, Chanderi brings comfort to the forefront without sacrificing refinement. Kapoor’s beauty look completes the narrative with her signature makeup. Coppery smoky eyes paired with nude lips that keep the focus on the ensemble. She left her hair open and styled with soft curls and gentle braids at the crown. She accessorised with a gold necklace, drop earrings and bracelets from Kalyan Jewellers. From the makeup to the anarkali, it is the kind of look that will transcend seasons and occasions, making a compelling case for year-long dressing that feels festive without being fleeting.

article_title: The best hairstyles for thin hair, according to experts
sub_title: Your cheat sheet to hair that looks twice as full in half the time
article_content: If you have thin hair and want a little extra lift, the right hairstyles for thin hair can make all the difference. The good thing about fine hair is that it’s surprisingly flexible: it styles quickly, takes well to heat, and doesn’t need a whole shelf of products to look sleek. The real challenge is We spoke to top stylists to break it down. Some hairstyles can add more oomph than others, especially if they give texture or height. “I find that encouraging movement and texture into the hair adds volume and stacks out the hair, which leads to making it look fuller and thicker,” says Reece Wentworth, stylist at Blue Tit Salon Clapton. “You can use wands, straighteners or whatever you feel most comfortable using to wrap the hair in different directions to create a tousled, textured look. You can also use a wide tooth comb to soften out the movement,” he says. Two great examples of hairstyles for fine hair are a blow dry and an updo. We also love half-up hair, since it gives the illusion of volume up top, while maintaining the length. A blow-dry gives thin hair more structure than air-drying ever will. Water weighs roots down. Lifting them as they TikTok has turned Half-up hair styles pull the top half of your crown section upward (hello, built-in lift) while leaving the rest of your length loose, so you get the best of both worlds. It breaks up the flatness you normally see when all the hair sits in one layer. A good cut can make a big difference to thin hair, by removing wisps and adding texture. But, no matter what style you go for, “keep it Fine-haired girls can sometimes struggle to make XXL lengths work since the ends can begin to look a little frayed and skimpy. So if you can't fight it, embracing a shorter style can give you the healthy hair you want. “I recommend regular haircuts,” says Reece. “Make sure not to latch onto the length. Having a haircut with a strong one-length and especially above the shoulder will make hair look thicker,” he says. Some of your best bets are bobs and lobs, face-framing layers and the Bardot fringe, if you're feeling especially adventurous. As long as you embrace your fine hair, you're golden.
